papers.title: From detection to decision: molecular, genomic, and AI innovations for managing Ganoderma boninense in oil palm.
papers.abstract: Ganoderma boninense causes basal stem rot (BSR) in oil palm, resulting in substantial economic losses, particularly for smallholders who contribute approximately 40% of global production. This review synthesizes advances in molecular diagnostic techniques (qPCR, LAMP), whole-genome sequencing of resistant Elaeis guineensis genotypes, and AI-driven remote sensing to enhance understanding of G. boninense pathobiology. Soilborne mycelia of the pathogen can persist for more than 10 y. Asymptomatic infections, which are frequently missed by conventional methods, can lead to significant disease spread within plantations over 2 y. CRISPR-based paper-strip tests have demonstrated high sensitivity (detecting < 1 pg DNA in laboratory settings), while marker-assisted selection has helped identify additional resistance QTLs. Trichoderma biofilms and biodegradable fumigants reduced soil inoculum by 50-75% in controlled studies. AI-based decision support systems have demonstrated promising accuracy for guiding interventions and potential cost savings, although further field validation across diverse conditions is needed.

papers.title: Multiscale and physically consistent multitask learning for protein melting temperature prediction.
papers.abstract: Protein thermal stability determines the functional viability of proteins in industrial and biomedical applications. We developed an Evolutionary Scale Modeling Cambrian-based multiscale multitask predictor for protein melting temperature (ESMTmP). The model leverages a frozen 300-million-parameter Cambrian encoder to extract residue representations. These features are refined by residual temporal convolutions. Furthermore, global statistical pooling, local multiscale convolutions, and multi-head attention are integrated through residual gated fusion. This framework unifies adaptive representation learning with continuous temperature regression and ordered multi-threshold classification. It also introduces monotonicity regularization to encourage order-consistent probability outputs. The model was trained on 30,076 observations and evaluated on 531 exact-identity-separated held-out proteins. ESMTmP achieved a root mean square error (RMSE) of 7.42 °C and a mean absolute error of 5.64 °C. Additionally, the coefficient of determination reached 0.8112 with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9014. Compared with an encoder baseline, the RMSE decreased from 7.87 to 7.42 °C. Multitask learning further reduced this error from 7.61 to 7.42 °C relative to a regression-only variant, demonstrating that auxiliary supervision effectively limits large prediction errors. Across five temperature thresholds from 40 to 80 °C, the mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve reached 0.9462. The mean F1 score was 0.8663 with no monotonicity violations. ESMTmP provides monotonically ordered predictions to efficiently prioritize thermostable protein engineering candidates prior to experimental screening. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05122-1.

papers.title: In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering.
papers.abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease 1 . Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model 2,3 . Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor-encapsulated within a GalNAc-lipid nanoparticle-leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

papers.title: Perspective. Precision Nutrition at a Crossroads: From Biological Prediction to Contextual Implementation.
papers.abstract: Precision nutrition has substantially reshaped nutritional science by demonstrating that individuals can respond differently to identical dietary exposures. Advances in genomics, metabolomics, proteomics, microbiome research, wearable technologies, digital health, and artificial intelligence have improved our ability to characterize biological heterogeneity and predict individual responses to diet. However, demonstrating such variability does not necessarily result in nutritional strategies that provide clinically meaningful benefits beyond established evidence-based care. A critical distinction should therefore be made between precision nutrition as a discovery science, which has convincingly established interindividual heterogeneity in dietary responses, and precision nutrition as an intervention science, which must demonstrate meaningful incremental value over dietary approaches already supported by clinical evidence. Despite increasingly sophisticated technologies and predictive models, evidence of consistent improvements in long-term health outcomes, cost-effectiveness, scalability, and equity remains limited. In this Perspective, we argue that precision nutrition has reached a critical crossroads. We distinguish prediction of individual responses, which is only one route to precision nutrition, from treatment-effect heterogeneity, treatment selection and clinical utility. We then propose contextual precision nutrition as a translational framework that integrates biological responsiveness with the behavioral, psychological, social, cultural, economic, and environmental determinants of dietary behavior. Rather than claiming novelty for these components, the framework integrates them into a decision logic that asks whether biological information improves the selection of a dietary strategy beyond routine information and established care, and how that strategy can be delivered and sustained. It complements population-based dietary recommendations by refining their implementation and maximizing adherence and real-world effectiveness. Ultimately, the success of precision nutrition will be determined not by the sophistication of its predictions but by its ability to translate biological knowledge into interventions that are clinically effective, scalable, equitable, and sustainable, thereby improving both individual and population health.

papers.title: Microenvironment of Bone and Joint Infection: Examining the Microenvironment.
papers.abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a major complication of arthroplasty, and conventional diagnostic methods for PJI remain limited by suboptimal sensitivity, long turnaround times, high cost, and patient inconvenience, particularly in biofilm-associated and culture-negative infections. Emerging data suggest that the infected joint microenvironment contains host- and pathogen-derived molecular signatures with substantial diagnostic potential. This review evaluates current evidence on microenvironment-related biomarkers in PJI, including host extracellular vesicles, host cell-free nucleic acids (microRNA/cell-free DNA), non-host-derived biomarkers, and sequencing-based pathogen detection techniques. Host-derived biomarkers show favorable discriminatory capability by characterizing inflammatory and immune responses, and metagenomic and sequencing-based technologies improve pathogen identification. Despite encouraging diagnostic performance, widespread clinical implementation remains limited due to a lack of standardization, cost, and limited prospective validation. Future prospective multicenter studies should integrate conventional microbiological methods with molecular and microenvironment-based approaches to improve diagnostic accuracy.

papers.title: Routine urinalysis-based machine learning framework for predicting urine culture contamination.
papers.abstract: Urine culture contamination is a common preanalytical challenge, yet conventional urinalysis strategies rarely treat it as an independent outcome. This retrospective study included 8446 specimens from 6686 patients, split at the patient level into training and internal validation sets. An additional 3481 specimens from 2819 patients at two other campuses of the same hospital system were used for external validation. Nineteen demographic and routine urinalysis variables were analyzed. We developed a two-stage XGBoost framework that first distinguished bacterial growth from negative culture and then contamination from pathogenic growth. Thresholds were selected during training to maintain ≥95% sensitivity for bacterial-growth detection in Stage 1 and ≥ 95% specificity for pathogenic growth in Stage 2. Comparators included one-stage three-class, class-weighted, and binary contamination-versus-rest XGBoost models and SEC-based rules. The binary contamination-versus-rest model and SEC-based rules showed limited contamination recall (0.411 [0.348-0.475] to 0.589 [0.525-0.651]). Relative to the two-stage reference, the one-stage three-class model had significantly lower contamination recall (0.572 versus 0.732) and pathogenic-growth recall (0.746 versus 0.901) in internal validation (both Holm-adjusted P < 0.001), whereas the class-weighted model achieved comparable contamination recall (0.765) but with reduced pathogenic-growth recall (0.741) and a higher pathogen-to-contamination error rate (0.091 versus 0.033). Decision curve analysis showed positive net benefit at both external sites. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified bacilli count, SEC, and WBC as the main contributors in Stage 2. This two-stage framework may support urine culture diagnostic stewardship by flagging approximately three-quarters of contaminated cultures before culture reporting. Prospective multicenter and cross-platform validation is needed before routine implementation.

papers.title: Evaluation of targets for normalization of viral pathogen concentrations in building dust.
papers.abstract: Building dust is potentially an important public health tool for monitoring human pathogens because it contains genetic material from pathogens. However, building dust is heterogeneous and presents technical challenges for environmental pathogen surveillance. To effectively use pathogen measurements in building dust for environmental surveillance, normalization procedures that account for human contribution to dust may be necessary and could help account for variability in occupancy and temporal resolution. Our analysis investigates potential indicators of human emission that could be used to normalize data on concentration of pathogens in dust. Ninety-nine vacuum dust samples were collected from 33 buildings and concentrations were measured for three emission indicators ( i.e. , human cytochrome B gene, Carjivirus communis (previously crAssphage), and pepper mild mottle virus) and two respiratory pathogens ( i.e. SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus). All of these were detected in ≥91% of the samples, with the exception of influenza A virus (73%). Most pairings of indicators (nine of 10) showed a weak to moderate positive correlation with one another (Kendall's τ ≤ 0.28). Correlations between occupancy and emission indicators and respiratory pathogens were weak (Kendall's τ < |0.15|) and non-significant ( p > 0.1). Among all potential markers, MT-CYB was most promising, with detection in 96% of the samples, higher concentration than others, and stronger correlation with other potential measures of occupancy.

papers.title: Genomic Profiling of the Virulence Potential and Antimicrobial Resistance of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli from Surface Water and Animal Sources.
papers.abstract: The aim of this work was to characterize the pathogenic potential of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) circulating in environmental and animal reservoirs. To achieve this, 225 genomes were analyzed: four genomes were obtained from bovine mastitis isolates, and 221 were obtained from the NCBI Pathogen Detection database originating from surface water and animal fecal samples. All genomes were analyzed to identify virulence-associated factors and antimicrobial resistance profiles in strains collected from surface water and animal samples. Virulence analysis revealed that stx1 and stx2 were detected in 32% and 44% of isolates, respectively. Environmental genomes frequently carried adhesion and LEE-associated genes, while mastitis isolates lacked these markers but exhibited enriched iron uptake systems and hemolysins, indicating niche-specific virulence repertoires. Resistance analysis identified 105 genes that contribute to antimicrobial resistance against multiple antibiotic families, including beta-lactams, quinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and polymyxins. Phylogenetic analysis classified the strains mainly into phylogroups B1 (63.56%) and E (28%), and serotyping identified 41 serotypes, with O157:H7 being the most common (25.33%). MLST revealed 46 STs, with ST11 being the predominant one in animal fecal isolates. Overall, the data indicate a genetically diverse STEC population, with shared lineages among water, feces, and mastitis, as well as combined virulence and multidrug resistance profiles. This supports the need to incorporate genomic surveillance in environmental and livestock reservoirs to anticipate and mitigate the risks of transmission to the human population.

papers.title: Single-Nucleus Transcriptomics Reveals Cell Type Specific Defence Responses and Identifies AhWRKY40 as a Key Regulator of Peanut Resistance to Sclerotium rolfsii.
papers.abstract: Peanut stem rot caused by Sclerotium rolfsii is a devastating soil borne disease that severely constrains peanut production worldwide. Despite its economic importance, highly resistant peanut cultivars are still largely unavailable, and the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying peanut resistance remain poorly understood. We obtained a total of 29,308 high-quality nuclei, annotated five major cell types, and detected 52,819 expressed genes. Comparative analysis revealed widespread transcriptional reprogramming and a predominance of downregulated genes in response to pathogen infection, accompanied by a substantial reduction in cell abundance across all cell populations. Notably, epidermal cells harboured the highest proportion of disease resistance genes. Pseudotime trajectory analysis further demonstrated that S. rolfsii infection altered cellular transcriptional states and induced cell type specific immune reprogramming. Integrative analyses combining gene coexpression, pseudotime dynamics, virtual knockout, and transgenic validation consistently identified AhWRKY40 as a key regulatory factor associated with disease resistance. Overexpression of AhWRKY40 enhanced resistance to S. rolfsii and was accompanied by increased accumulation of jasmonic acid (JA) and salicylic acid (SA), suggesting its involvement in hormone-mediated defence responses. Collectively, our study provides new insights into the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying peanut resistance to stem rot, identifies AhWRKY40 as a promising candidate gene for disease resistance, and establishes a valuable resource for functional genomics and molecular breeding to improve southern blight resistance in peanut.

papers.title: Off-panel resistance determinants in a high-resistance setting: comparative evaluation of syndromic multiplex PCR, metagenomic sequencing, and phenotypic AST in bloodstream infections.
papers.abstract: Rapid syndromic molecular panels substantially reduce turnaround time for bloodstream infection diagnosis by identifying common pathogens and selected antimicrobial resistance determinants directly from positive blood cultures. However, their fixed target repertoires may limit diagnostic coverage in settings with diverse endemic resistance mechanisms and clinically relevant off-panel organisms. This retrospective comparative diagnostic study evaluated direct-from-positive-blood-culture metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), the BioFire Blood Culture Identification 2 (BCID2) panel, and routine microbiological methods across 165 positive blood-culture episodes from 145 patients at a tertiary-care center with a high burden of antimicrobial resistance. Complete recovery of the routine-culture organism set was achieved in 155/165 episodes (93.9%) by mNGS and 142/165 (86.1%) by BCID2. Among 23 episodes with incomplete routine-set recovery by BCID2, mNGS restored complete coverage in 18 (78.3%). For meropenem resistance, sensitivity was numerically higher with mNGS than with BCID2 (90.0% versus 75.0%), whereas ceftriaxone-resistance sensitivity among Enterobacterales was numerically higher with BCID2 (97.5% versus 85.0%); neither paired difference was statistically significant. BCID2 meropenem very major errors were concentrated among non-fermenting gram-negative organisms, particularly Acinetobacter baumannii , and were frequently associated with off-panel bla OXA-23 detected by mNGS. Overall, targeted syndromic testing and mNGS demonstrated complementary diagnostic performance, with mNGS extending organism and resistance-mechanism coverage beyond predefined molecular targets, while phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing remained necessary for definitive susceptibility assessment.IMPORTANCERapid molecular blood-culture panels provide clinically actionable results, but are inherently restricted to predefined pathogen and resistance targets. This limitation is particularly relevant in regions where local antimicrobial resistance epidemiology includes mechanisms not represented within commercial panel repertoires. In this study, metagenomic sequencing improved recovery of routine-culture organisms and identified off-panel carbapenem resistance determinants underlying several false-susceptible panel results, particularly OXA-23 in Acinetobacter baumannii . However, broader genomic detection did not consistently improve phenotypic resistance prediction across antimicrobial classes. These findings illustrate that diagnostic breadth and phenotypic predictive accuracy are distinct attributes and support the use of metagenomic sequencing as a complementary approach to rapid targeted testing and conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing.

papers.title: From Genomics to Diagnostics: Combating the Spread of Vascular Streak Dieback in North America.
papers.abstract: Vascular streak dieback (VSD) has emerged as a major threat to woody ornamental production in the United States (U.S.), currently affecting at least 50 tree and shrub species across 25 botanical genera in at least twelve U.S. states. The putative causal agent, here termed the VSD-associated Ceratobasidiaceae lineage (Csp), presents diagnostic challenges due to its fastidious growth requirements and vascular colonization pattern. Here, we integrate genomics-guided marker discovery with multi-platform genome-anchored tools (SSR, TaqMan qPCR, and LAMP that target unique genomic regions identified through comparative genomics) to deliver a field-deployable, genome-anchored toolkit for detection and genotyping of Csp across nurseries and landscapes. We evaluated the performance of these tools using 103 samples representing DNA isolated from 64 VSD-symptomatic plants or their fungal isolates and 39 non-target Ceratobasidiaceae outgroups. Genome assembly of Illumina reads yielded ten informative microsatellite markers with an overall amplification success rate of 95.8% (91.7%-100.0% across Csp samples). These markers demonstrated strong performance in distinguishing the Csp samples from the outgroups. Among the three TaqMan probes developed, VSD048 exhibited superior performance with 100% detection across Csp samples, characterized by cycle threshold (C T ) values of 26.8 ± 4.2, and no cross-reactivity with C. theobromae or other Ceratobasidiaceae species. A multi-laboratory ring trial confirmed the reproducibility of the VSD048 TaqMan assay across various testing platforms. The loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay targeting the Csp-unique region achieved a sensitivity of 0.82 [95% CI 0.68-0.968] and specificity of 1.00 [95% CI 1.00-1.00], with a practical detection threshold of approximately 25 copies of the target region. Our molecular survey of the disease revealed a surprisingly broad host range beyond Cercis canadensis (Eastern redbud), encompassing eight additional genera, and confirmed its geographical distribution across the eastern and midwestern U.S. These validated molecular tools provide rapid, sensitive, and specific detection methods for Csp surveillance and management. The field-applicable LAMP assay and laboratory-based TaqMan/SSR protocols offer complementary approaches for different diagnostic scenarios, thereby enabling early detection and supporting efforts to limit the spread of this emerging pathogen in nursery and landscape settings.

papers.title: How Stroke Genetics Is Impacting Clinical Care: Now and the Future.
papers.abstract: The past decade has seen a transformation in our understanding of the genetics of stroke. However, a commonly asked question is how do these advances impact the practicing clinician now, and what are their implications for clinical care in the future? This review outlines the major recent advances in stroke genetics and addresses 4 questions most relevant to the clinician: What do we now know about the genetic architecture of stroke? When and how should genetic testing be used to identify monogenic stroke? How can genetic information be applied to risk stratification and prevention? And what therapeutic implications are emerging from genetic discoveries? It highlights the success of genome-wide association studies in stroke and how these have transformed how we understand the genetic architecture of stroke. An increasing number of monogenic forms of cerebral small vessel disease are being identified, and guidance on when and how to test for them is covered. Polygenic risk scores are gaining increasing attention. How these can be applied, and the challenges in their use are discussed. Lastly, the impact of genomics on stroke therapeutics, whether by identifying new targets, assessing causality using techniques such as Mendelian randomization, or pharmacogenomics, is discussed.

papers.title: An Enzyme-Mediated Duplex Exponential Amplification Assay for Rapid Detection of Plasmodiophora brassicae .
papers.abstract: Clubroot, caused by the soilborne obligate biotrophic protist Plasmodiophora brassicae , substantially reduces the yield and quality of cruciferous crops worldwide. In this study, an enzyme-mediated duplex exponential amplification (EmDEA) assay was developed for rapid detection of P. brassicae in extracted DNA. By comparing the P. brassicae strain 3A genome with representative bacterial, fungal, and oomycete genome assemblies, we identified 157 candidate regions that showed no detectable matches in the selected non-target genomes under the specified alignment criteria. Pbspec1, a fragment within the annotated locus PBTT_08698, was selected based on computational non-target screening, within-species conservation, and suitability for assay design. PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing were used to validate the target fragment. Six forward primers, six reverse primers, and six RNA probes were screened, and F2-R4-RNA2 was selected for subsequent EmDEA experiments. Using serial dilutions of purified recombinant plasmid DNA, the F2-R4-RNA2 combination consistently detected template concentrations of 1.0 × 10 3 copies/μL and above. No amplification was observed from the 12 non-target fungal or bacterial organisms. The assay detected P. brassicae in DNA extracted from four infected root samples and three naturally infested soil samples. All tested positive samples produced detectable fluorescence during a programmed 20-min run on a portable isothermal fluorescence instrument. These results support the potential use of EmDEA for rapid preliminary screening of P. brassicae following DNA extraction.

papers.title: Evaluation of ITS copy number variation among Clarireedia jacksonii isolates using single-copy genetic markers cam and hsp60 .
papers.abstract: Molecular tools are widely used for plant pathogen detection and quantification. Recent quantitative PCR applications for the turfgrass disease causal agent Clarireedia jacksonii were developed targeting the ITS region and showed potential utility in improved disease management. However, accurate and consistent pathogen quantification is contingent on stable copy numbers of the target genes across populations. In this study, we evaluated the genomic copy number of molecular markers in C. jacksonii using in silico analyses, quantitative PCR, and digital PCR. Calmodulin ( cam ), elongation factor 1-alpha ( ef1α ), and minichromosome maintenance protein 7 ( mcm7 ) were consistently identified as single-copy loci, whereas ITS exhibited multiple copies in two out of nine assemblies. Digital PCR confirmed that cam and heat shock protein 60 ( hsp60 ) closely followed theoretical single-copy expectations across a genomic DNA dilution series of C. jacksonii isolate HRS10. In the analysis of 27 C. jacksonii isolates, ITS was consistently detected as a multicopy locus, with copy number estimates ranging from 33 to 48 copies per genome when normalized using cam and from 34 to 52 copies per genome when normalized using hsp60 . These results demonstrate that ITS copy number variation among C. jacksonii isolates was consistently observed, independent of the single-copy reference locus used for normalization. Therefore, single-copy genetic markers, such as cam and hsp60 , may represent superior choices for accurate and stable estimation of fungal genome equivalents in C. jacksonii .

papers.title: Molecular detection of Coxiella burnetii and a Coxiellaceae bacterium in Hyalomma asiaticum and Dermacentor nuttalli ticks collected in Mongolia.
papers.abstract: Coxiella burnetii, the causative agent of Q fever, is a zoonotic pathogen for which epidemiological data are limited in Mongolia. This study investigated the presence of C. burnetii in ticks collected across Mongolia from forest, pasture, and livestock-associated environments. A total of 7,511 ticks were collected from 42 Soums across 12 provinces and 2 districts of Ulaanbaatar between May and June 2018. Molecular detection of Coxiella-related organisms was performed using 46 DNA samples, comprising 28 individual-tick samples and 18 pooled-tick samples representing 489 ticks, by nested PCR targeting IS1111 and the 16S rRNA gene. Twenty DNA samples (2 individual ticks and 18 pools) were PCR-positive. Sequencing and phylogenetic analysis revealed that 9 Hyalomma asiaticum tick pools contained 16S rRNA sequences of C. burnetii, whereas 11 Dermacentor nuttalli samples (2 individual ticks and 9 pools) contained 16S rRNA sequences of a Coxiellaceae bacterium. Two individual D. nuttalli ticks yielded IS1111 sequences closely related to C. burnetii, whereas the corresponding 16S rRNA sequences clustered with a Coxiellaceae bacterium, highlighting discordance between the 2 molecular targets. The C. burnetii sequences detected in H. asiaticum were closely related to clade A strains reported from the United States, Japan, Greenland, and Korea, whereas sequences detected in D. nuttalli clustered with Coxiella endosymbiont sequences. This study provides molecular evidence for the presence of C. burnetii in H. asiaticum tick pools in Mongolia and demonstrates that Mongolian ticks harbor genetically diverse Coxiella-related bacteria, highlighting the need for further investigation of their epidemiological significance.

papers.title: Educational framework to strengthen the variant scientist workforce in clinical genomics.
papers.abstract: The integration of genomics into clinical care has created an urgent need for accurate, standardized variant interpretation. Variant Scientists (VSs) play a central role in translating sequencing results into clinically actionable findings, yet formal education and standardized training pathways for this emerging profession are still evolving internationally. This study aimed to describe educational needs of practicing VSs and to develop a structured training program informed by those needs. A national survey was distributed to practicing VSs across Israeli clinical genetics centers to assess training background, learning, access to interpretation tools, and professional challenges. Survey findings informed the definition of core competencies and the development of a phased training program by a multidisciplinary working group. Thirty-eight respondents were included. Professional training was mostly acquired through observation of expert analysts (42.1%), followed by hands-on experience (39.5%). Only 18.4% participated in a dedicated VS course. Key challenges included keeping pace with evolving guidelines (55.3%) and copy number variant (CNV) analysis (47.4%). The survey identified substantial variability in training pathways and highlighted priority areas for structured education. Based on these findings, a structured training program was developed, combining theoretical modules, practical training, and assessment via a standardized proficiency test, supported by institutional forums and national meetings. This study presents a structured, scalable VS training program informed by a national needs assessment. By aligning the curriculum with identified educational needs, it provides a practical model that may support more standardized VS training and inform similar initiatives in clinical genomics internationally.

papers.title: Detection of common neonatal sepsis pathogens using a contemporary pediatric blood culture system.
papers.abstract: To evaluate recovery and time to positivity (TTP) of neonatal sepsis pathogens at low and ultra-low organism concentrations using a contemporary pediatric automated blood culture system. Six common neonatal sepsis pathogens were prepared in a 1:1 mixture of donor whole blood and saline-organism suspension at final concentrations ranging from ≤1 to 10-20 CFU/mL. Aliquots of 0.25-2.0 mL, containing 0.125-1.0 mL donor whole blood, were inoculated into BD BACTEC Peds Plus/F bottles. Recovery and TTP were assessed. Clinically important neonatal pathogens remained recoverable at very low inocula, including ≤1 CFU/mL. Median TTP ranged from 10 to 12 h for Escherichia coli and Streptococcus agalactiae to 20-26 h for coagulase-negative staphylococci. Increasing organism concentration shortened TTP for E. coli, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus capitis, and S. agalactiae. Inoculated suspension volume had relatively little effect on TTP among recovered cultures. Recovery improved across larger inoculated suspension volumes, particularly for staphylococcal organisms. A contemporary pediatric blood culture system demonstrated excellent recovery of common neonatal sepsis pathogens, including at very low organism concentrations. Larger inoculated suspension volumes primarily improved pathogen recovery rather than substantially faster detection. These findings support optimizing and documenting blood culture specimen volume as part of neonatal diagnostic stewardship. Common neonatal sepsis pathogens remained recoverable at very low organism concentrations, including ≤1 CFU/mL, using a contemporary pediatric blood culture system. Organism-specific differences in time to positivity were more pronounced than the generally modest effects of organism concentration or inoculated suspension volume. Larger inoculated suspension volumes primarily improved pathogen recovery rather than detection speed. Recovery of staphylococci was reduced at smaller inoculated suspension volumes, particularly at ultra-low organism concentrations. These findings support attention to specimen volume and documentation of the volume obtained as components of neonatal diagnostic and antimicrobial stewardship.

papers.title: PmiREN3.0: a multi-omics integrated and AI-assisted encyclopedia for plant microRNA research.
papers.abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators in gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Comprehensive research on miRNAs increasingly requires the integration of large and heterogeneous datasets, together with more efficient approaches to knowledge exploration. Here, we present PmiREN3.0, a major update of the Plant MicroRNA Encyclopedia. Compared with PmiREN2.0, species/subspecies coverage increased from 179 to 340, adding 22 orders, 51 families, and 108 genera. Using the same standardized workflow and annotation criteria as previous releases, high-confidence miRNAs were identified from 5319 small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets, with miRNA loci increasing from 39 751 to 87 667 and miRNA families from 7838 to 18 389. Resources and tools from previous releases were extensively updated, while six new modules were added for primary transcripts, DNA methylation, RNA modifications, stress-responsive expression, metabolic pathways, and core GRNs. PmiREN3.0 also introduces miRai+, a knowledge service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines a language model fine-tuned on miRNA knowledge with retrieval augmented generation. Evaluation yielded scores of 0.910 for answer relevance, 0.965 for faithfulness, and 0.906 for factual correctness. Together, PmiREN3.0 provides an expanded plant miRNA dataset and an integrated platform combining multi-omics data and AI-assisted knowledge services for plant miRNA research. PmiREN3.0 is available at https://pmiren.com/.

papers.title: Simpler is not always better: Phylodynamic misspecification and deep-learning corrections.
papers.abstract: Phylodynamics bridges the gap between epidemiology and pathogen genetic data. The birth-death (BD) model and its extensions serve to infer the average number of secondary infections Re and the infection duration d from time-scaled pathogen phylogenies. Moreover, more complex models add extra parameters, such as the average length of the incubation period, the proportion of superspreaders in the infected population, or the speed-up in detection after contact-tracing. However, these additional parameters come at an important computational cost: While the simplest, BD, model, has a closed-form solution, its extensions do not and require numerical methods for their likelihood computation. This leads to increased computational times and potential numerical errors. Therefore, the BD model remains the favorite researchers'choice for real dataset analyses, and is often applied even in cases where more complex epidemiological aspects are present. We investigated, using simulations, how model misspecification influences inference of Re and d in the phylodynamic framework. We showed that the use of models not accounting for various epidemiological aspects leads to bias. In particular the simplest, BD, estimator tends to underestimate Re in the presence of super-spreading, incubation or contact-tracing, which might be dangerous from the public health perspective. In contrast, deep-learning-based estimators for complex models, accounting for multiple epidemiological factors, performed well in our simulations both on the data where those factors were present and where they were absent. This motivates the use of complex epidemiologically realistic estimators, whose design has recently become possible thanks to deep learning.

papers.title: Cotton Cultivar Effects on DNA-Based Quantification of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum Race 4 in Soil.
papers.abstract: The soilborne fungal pathogen Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum race 4 (FOV4) poses a risk to U.S. cotton ( Gossypium spp.) following detection in California, Texas, and New Mexico. This study evaluated the influence of cotton cultivar resistance on relative variation in soil FOV4 DNA quantity, a proxy for inoculum density, in a naturally infested field over 2 years. Field trials included Upland ( G. hirsutum ) and Pima ( G. barbadense ) cotton cultivars and measured plant mortality, root necrosis, and lint yield. Bulk soil FOV4 DNA was quantified by qPCR at three timepoints each year: planting, midseason (first flower), and late season (crop maturity). Susceptible Pima cultivars exhibited the highest mortality, most severe necrosis, and lowest yields, whereas resistant Pima and Upland cultivars had lower necrosis with variable mortality and yield. Commercial Upland cultivars with differing degrees of susceptibility showed intermediate mortality and necrosis yet high yields. Midseason soil FOV4 DNA levels varied among cultivars in both years ( P = 0.011, 0.028), with elevated levels in a subset of susceptible cultivars. Late season DNA levels varied among cultivars in 2021 ( P = 0.017) but not in 2020 ( P = 0.080) and did not correspond to resistance designations. Within cultivars, mortality correlated with FOV4 DNA levels at planting ( P < 0.001, McFadden's pseudo- R 2 [ R 2 MF ] = 0.810) and late season ( P < 0.001, R 2 MF = 0.802), necrosis with late season DNA levels ( P < 0.001, R 2 = 0.849), and yield showed no correlation with FOV4 DNA at any timepoint. These findings relate host response to DNA-based soil pathogen quantification and emphasize resistance variation as a determinant of FOV4 disease ecology and management success.

papers.title: Global Population Genomics Links Mobilome Architecture to Antimicrobial Resistance Gene Burden in Pseudomonas aeruginosa .
papers.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a critical opportunistic pathogen responsible for severe healthcare-associated infections globally. Understanding its population structure and the interplay between antimicrobial resistance, mobile genetic elements (mobilome), and virulence profiles is essential for combating its spread. This study analyzes 7,341 quality-filtered P. aeruginosa genomes from 84 countries to define the global population structure and characterize the relationships between the mobilome, antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) burden, and virulence profiles. Using a consensus resistome approach alongside specialized bioinformatic tools for mobile genetic elements and virulence factors, we found that the global population exhibits extensive genomic diversity alongside prominent international high-risk clones like ST235 and ST111. Acquired-candidate ARG burden was most strongly associated with integron-related features, whereas insertion sequence metrics showed moderate unadjusted correlations, with no independent association for total IS count after multivariable adjustment. Plasmid-associated metrics showed comparatively weaker associations. While virulence-associated gene content remains largely conserved across the population, type III secretion system effectors exoU and exoS display a largely reciprocal and lineage-specific distribution. Furthermore, carbapenemase genes show distinct geographic and clonal patterns, highlighting a dual dynamic of international high-risk clone dissemination and regional acquisition. These findings are consistent with a major contribution of mobile genetic elements to ARG accumulation in P. aeruginosa , emphasizing the need for continuous genomic surveillance to track and contain emerging strains.

papers.title: Comparative genomic and resistome analysis of Citrobacter koseri: first genome report from Egypt.
papers.abstract: Citrobacter koseri is increasingly implicated in healthcare- and community-associated infections, with multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains posing a growing clinical concern. However, its population structure and resistome dynamics remain incompletely understood. Here, we report the first draft genome sequence of an MDR C. koseri isolate (DFU32) from Egypt, recovered from a patient with a diabetic foot ulcer (DFU). We also present a comparative genomic and resistome analysis of 518 publicly available C. koseri genomes available at the time of the study. The isolate exhibited resistance to multiple antimicrobial classes, including β-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and sulfonamides, as well as tigecycline and colistin. MLST assigned DFU32 to sequence type (ST) 1172. Genomic analysis identified 21 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, including multiple β-lactamases (bla CKO , bla TEM , bla OXA-9 , bla CTX-M-15 , and bla CMY-2 ) and aminoglycoside resistance determinants, including armA. Colistin resistance was associated with the presence of a PhoQ V381I substitution. Comparative analysis of 518 publicly available genomes revealed 140 unique AMR genes across the species, with 73.6% of genomes carrying acquired resistance determinants. The population comprised two major lineages, bla CKO and bla MAL , with the MAL lineage, particularly MAL-2, carrying significantly more AMR genes. Carbapenemase genes were identified in 29.1% of genomes and were distributed across nearly half of the detected STs, with bla KPC variants predominating. Mobilized colistin resistance (mcr) genes were detected in 2.5% of genomes. Both carbapenemase and mcr genes were predominantly located on plasmid-associated contigs. Notably, chromosomal integration events were observed. These included mcr-9.1, which was associated with IS26 and IS903B, and bla KPC-2 , which was embedded within an IS26-bracketed transposon (IS26-recA-ISKpn27-bla KPC-2 -ISKpn6-IS26) in novel STs. These findings underscore the genomic plasticity of C. koseri and the potential for stable, plasmid-independent maintenance of colistin and carbapenem resistance. Among the identified STs, ST690 displayed a particularly high resistance gene load, including carbapenemase and mcr genes, suggesting that it may represent a high-risk lineage. This study provides the first genome-based characterization of an MDR C. koseri isolate from Egypt. The results highlight the potential genetic mobility and global spread of AMR determinants in this emerging pathogen. Notably, the studied isolate was recovered from DFU, underscoring the increasing clinical relevance of C. koseri in chronic wound infections.

papers.title: Advances in assessing donor organ quality and perioperative risk for kidney transplantation.
papers.abstract: Kidney transplantation faces persistent challenges in accurately evaluating donor organ quality and predicting long-term outcomes, with traditional assessment methods demonstrating limited predictive capacity. The increasing utilization of marginal-quality donor organs has intensified the need for sophisticated evaluation strategies. Machine perfusion technology has transformed organ preservation from mere static storage to a dynamic platform potentially enabling real-time monitoring, assessment, and interventions during the preservation period. Molecular profiling technologies such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics could provide refined biomarkers for donor kidney assessment across several phases of kidney transplantation. The first window arises during donor evaluation. Techniques such as high-resolution molecular typing, genetic profiling, epigenomic markers, and artificial intelligence-enhanced imaging provide additional information compared to traditional scoring systems. During organ preservation, a second window emerges, allowing additional, isolated assessment of the organ after procurement but before transplantation. Machine perfusion systems enable sampling of perfusate and tissue for multi-omics analysis to characterize injury or function, although most candidate biomarkers remain at the discovery or early validation stage. After transplantation, donor-derived cell-free deoxyribonucleic acid, urinary chemokines, and advanced imaging modalities offer non-invasive early detection of graft injury. Clinical translation of these new techniques faces substantial challenges: most studies are single-center and have small sample sizes, assay standardization remains incomplete, and evidence linking biomarker-guided decisions to improved long-term graft survival is lacking. Machine learning may enhance risk stratification but remains largely unvalidated in prospective trials. Future progress requires a shift from short-term endpoint prediction to long-term outcome validation through multicenter studies, standardized protocols, and equitable implementation strategies.

papers.title: Future directions and challenges of drug development and non-human primate models.
papers.abstract: Gene and cell therapy are transforming therapeutic approaches for genetic diseases and malignancies. This review examines the current role and future directions of non-human primate (NHP) models in preclinical safety evaluation of adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapy and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy amid accelerating adoption of new approach methodologies (NAMs). We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure for publications from January 2015 to June 2026; approximately 60 English-language and 5 Chinese-language publications, together with FDA, EMA, and NMPA guidance documents, were included. NHPs remain the reference species for AAV and CAR-T safety evaluation, yet supply crises, ethical pressures, and documented prediction gaps (hepatotoxicity, dorsal root ganglion injury) are driving NAMs adoption. Organoids, organs-on-chips (87% sensitivity and 100% specificity for drug-induced liver injury), and AI-driven models are maturing under the FDA Modernization Act 2.0 and the 2025 FDA roadmap. We propose the Hierarchical Replacement Assessment Framework (HRAF), a three-tier, two-threshold model that reallocates NHP resources from routine screening to risk confirmation, providing an actionable roadmap for mechanism-based and welfare-conscious preclinical development.

papers.title: Structural Diversity and Functional Roles of the Internalin Family Proteins in Listeria monocytogenes.
papers.abstract: Listeria monocytogenes is an important foodborne intracellular pathogen that can cause listeriosis in humans and animals, with a relatively high mortality rate. Internalin (Inl) family proteins are critical virulence factors of L. monocytogenes and play essential roles in bacterial adhesion, host cell invasion, tissue colonization, immune evasion, and systemic infection. In recent years, with the continuous advancement of genomics, structural biology, and host-pathogen interaction studies, an increasing number of internalin family members and their biological functions have been identified. Different internalins exhibit significant differences in receptor recognition, tissue tropism, and pathogenic mechanisms. This review systematically summarizes the structural characteristics and classification of the internalin family in L. monocytogenes, with particular emphasis on recent advances in the functions of major family members, including InlA, InlB, InlC, InlK, InlF, InlP, InlL, and InlJ, in intestinal invasion, penetration of the placental and blood-brain barriers, intracellular survival, immune evasion, biofilm formation, and host interactions. Furthermore, recent research hotspots in the functional characterization of internalin proteins are discussed, along with their potential applications in elucidating virulence mechanisms, vaccine development, and targeted prevention and control strategies. This review aims to provide a theoretical reference for further investigations into the pathogenic mechanisms of L. monocytogenes and the development of novel prevention and control strategies.

papers.title: BioDecryptors, a Bioinformatics Escape Game for Undergraduate and Postgraduate Learners in Clinical Microbiology: Prospective Before-and-After Study.
papers.abstract: Bioinformatics is increasingly important in clinical microbiology with growing use of genomic sequencing, metagenomics, and phylogenetic analyses. However, introducing bioinformatics concepts and tools to medical learners can be challenging. Gamified educational approaches may allow introducing these concepts while supporting learner motivation. This study prospectively evaluated BioDecryptors, an educational escape game to introduce bioinformatics principles and tools in clinical microbiology, by assessing short-term changes in knowledge and self-reported motivation and evaluating participant satisfaction. We conducted a prospective before-and-after study between January and September 2025. Volunteers were recruited from undergraduate medical programs at Université Paris Cité and postgraduate programs or training activities for MDs and PharmDs at Université de Nantes, Université Paris-Saclay, and the French Society for Microbiology. Overall, 55 participants were included: 22 (40%) second-year medical students and 33 (60%) postgraduate MDs or PharmDs. Participants completed BioDecryptors in teams of 3 to 4 using versions adapted to their training level. Knowledge was assessed before and immediately after the activity using 2 distinct 10-item tests assessing the same predefined learning objectives. Motivation was assessed using a 12-item, 5-point Likert questionnaire covering 3 predefined domains, and satisfaction was assessed after the activity. Pre-post knowledge scores were compared using paired t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, as appropriate. Motivation items were analyzed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Statistical significance was defined as a 2-sided P <.05. Paired knowledge assessments were available for 50 participants. Mean knowledge scores increased from 7.0 (SD 2.0; 95% CI 6.4-7.5) before the activity to 7.9 (SD 2.0; 95% CI 7.4-8.5) afterward ( P <.001). The mean change was 0.93 (SD 1.39; 95% CI 0.26-1.60) points among undergraduates and 0.83 (SD 1.21; 95% CI 0.38-1.27) points among postgraduates, with no statistically significant between-group difference ( P =.79). Motivation increased for perceived usefulness ( P =.04), willingness to learn ( P =.01), understanding of bioinformatics in diseases ( P =.002), and confidence in bioinformatics abilities ( P =.002). Curiosity ( P =.46) and interest in real-life applications ( P =.33) did not significantly change. Among 50 satisfaction respondents, overall satisfaction was high (mean 4.7, SD 0.5; 95% CI 4.6-4.9); 98% (48/49) of the respondents to the corresponding item indicated an interest in other escape game modules. Participation in BioDecryptors was associated with short-term increases in bioinformatics knowledge and self-reported motivation, together with high participant satisfaction. Unlike previously reported escape games focusing primarily on clinical or infection-control topics, BioDecryptors integrates hands-on bioinformatics analyses into a clinical microbiology scenario and offers versions adapted to undergraduate and postgraduate learners. Our findings provide preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility and acceptability of this approach as a complementary educational resource for introducing bioinformatics in health professions training. Controlled studies with longer-term assessments are needed to establish its comparative educational effectiveness and knowledge retention.

papers.title: Nitroxoline treatment of Balamuthia mandrillaris triggers genomic crisis, transcriptional collapse, and incomplete encystment via copper and iron chelation.
papers.abstract: Balamuthia mandrillaris is a free-living amoeba that can infect the central nervous system to cause granulomatous amebic encephalitis (GAE), a fatal disease with mortality rates up to 90%. GAE is typically treated with a six-drug regimen with limited efficacy and significant toxicity. Our lab previously identified nitroxoline, a quinolone antibiotic, as a promising therapeutic complement to the existing regimen, and in 2021 nitroxoline was first successfully used to treat a human patient. In this study, we elucidate nitroxoline's mechanism of action using a combination of genomics, transcriptomics, chemical complementation, growth assays, and electron microscopy. In service of this goal, an annotated draft genome of B. mandrillaris strain CDC:V039 was generated using long read sequencing, yielding over 32,000 predicted protein coding sequences, the majority of which were present on telomere-to-telomere predicted chromosomal contigs. Leveraging this resource, comparative transcriptomics were used to characterize encystment responses to three different cellular stressors: nitroxoline, galactose, and hypoxia. Our findings reveal that nitroxoline-induced cysts undergo transcriptional collapse and genomic and structural destabilization via copper and iron chelation, and that preformed cysts are also disrupted by nitroxoline. These data provide insight into nitroxoline's multifaceted impact on B. mandrillaris growth and cellular processes and advance our understanding of the transcriptional landscape associated with stress induced encystment. Our findings support the continued clinical study of nitroxoline as a complement to the existing regimen.

papers.title: Novel Biomarkers for Bacterial Meningitis and Other Central Nervous System Infections.
papers.abstract: Timely and accurate diagnosis of central nervous system (CNS) infections remains challenging because of nonspecific clinical characteristics and limited diagnostic accuracy of conventional tests. Novel cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers may improve early diagnosis and facilitate differentiation between infectious aetiologies. This review summarizes established and emerging CSF biomarkers for the diagnosis of CNS infections, with a focus on bacterial meningitis, and discusses their potential clinical application. Several novel CSF biomarkers have demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance for bacterial meningitis. Among these, CSF C-reactive protein (CRP) has recently been implemented in clinical practice, while heparin-binding protein and combinations of CSF CRP with inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1β show similarly high diagnostic accuracy. Pathogen-specific biomarkers, including CXCL13 for neuroborreliosis and β-D-glucan and galactomannan for fungal CNS infections, further expand the diagnostic repertoire. In addition, multi-omics approaches, including metabolomics, lipidomics, and proteomics, have identified promising candidates such as pyruvate and phosphatidylcholines, although these require further validation. Untargeted techniques, including metagenomic next-generation sequencing and phage immunoprecipitation sequencing, further enhance pathogen detection and may complement microbiological testing. Novel biomarkers have the potential to substantially improve the diagnosis of CNS infections. Several biomarkers for bacterial meningitis are already available for clinical implementation, particularly in patients with intermediate CSF leukocyte counts, where diagnostic uncertainty is greatest. For viral and other CNS infections biomarkers remain scarce. Future studies should focus on validation of emerging biomarkers and on integrating biomarker panels with advanced molecular diagnostic techniques to enable rapid, accurate and clinically applicable diagnostic strategies.

papers.title: Comparative genomics and machine learning reveal antimicrobial resistance landscapes, population structures, and geographic signatures of pork-associated Salmonella Derby across major producing countries.
papers.abstract: Salmonella Derby is a major pork-associated foodborne pathogen, yet its genomic diversity across pork-producing countries has not been systematically compared. This study aimed to compare antimicrobial resistance (AMR) landscapes, population structures, and geographic genomic signatures. We analyzed all publicly available pork-associated genomes in the National Center for Biotechnology Information Pathogen Detection database (January 2025) from China (n = 235), France (n = 83), Mexico (n = 38), and the United States (n = 109), using co-occurrence and pairwise association analyses, core-genome phylogeny, and a random forest classifier trained on pan-genome gene presence/absence. Chinese isolates carried the most AMR determinants (15.3 per isolate), followed by Mexican (7.6), French (3.5), and American (3.0) isolates; this difference, and most country-associated AMR genes (ARGs), persisted within sequence type 40 (ST40). Moreover, fosA7.3 and tet(A) were hub ARGs in all countries, and in France ARG and virulence gene profiles were almost perfectly partitioned between ST39 and ST40. Phylogenetic analysis resolved two clades separated by 37,107-38,674 core-genome single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs); the dominant subclade was overwhelmingly ST40. One American ST40 isolate differed by only 18-20 SNPs from three French ST40 isolates. The classifier discriminated country with accuracy of 0.93-0.99 across 21 training:testing splits, remaining ≥ 0.96 when closely related isolates (≤ 10 SNPs) were kept in the same partition; an unannotated gene cluster (group 52) and the efflux pump gene acrF were the most informative features. These findings show strong country-level genomic structuring in pork-associated S. Derby, with implications for global surveillance and source attribution.

papers.title: Nationwide clinical-genomic epidemiology of listeriosis in Taiwan, 2018-2025: disease manifestations in relation to clonal background.
papers.abstract: Listeriosis is an uncommon but severe foodborne infection, yet nationwide data linking pathogen genomics with clinical manifestations remain limited. We analyzed 1,252 laboratory-confirmed symptomatic listeriosis cases reported through nationwide surveillance in Taiwan during 2018-2025, with whole-genome sequencing of the corresponding clinical Listeria monocytogenes isolate from every case. The average annual incidence was 6.68 cases per 1,000,000 person-years, and 30-day all-cause mortality was 11.4%. Incidence showed an age-dependent sex pattern, with higher incidence among females aged 15-44 years and a shift toward male predominance at older ages. The female excess at ages 15-44 years persisted after exclusion of documented maternal-neonatal cases (male-to-female incidence rate ratio, 0.57; 95% confidence interval, 0.36-0.89). Clonal complex 87 (CC87) was the predominant CC (35.9%), whereas CC1 and CC2 were associated with higher odds of central nervous system (CNS) infection. LIPI-4 occurred predominantly in CC87, and LIPI-4-positive isolates showed lower odds of CNS infection; however, this association could not be separated from clonal background. More broadly, most associations of pathogenicity islands, virulence genes, and their alleles with disease manifestations could not be separated from the underlying clonal backgrounds in which these markers occurred, and none of the estimable associations remained significant after CC adjustment. This nationwide clinical-genomic study characterizes the contemporary burden of listeriosis in Taiwan and highlights clonal background as essential context for interpreting associations between virulence markers and disease manifestations.

papers.title: Seasonal variation in chytrid infection in a stream-dwelling frog in Southern Brazil.
papers.abstract: Many wildlife disease systems exhibit pronounced seasonal dynamics driven by environmental conditions that modulate pathogen growth and host susceptibility. The aquatic fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), which infects and threatens amphibians worldwide, presents a seasonal infection pattern linked to different factors that drive disease outbreaks and population decline. Here, we investigated seasonal and individual variation in Bd infection in the stream-dwelling frog Limnomedusa macroglossa, which inhabits rocky outcrops in southern Brazil. A seasonal infection peak was detected, with higher prevalence and infection loads during the cold months, and temperature was an important predictor of Bd detection probability. Individuals that exhibited infection peaks during the cold season showed a marked reduction or complete clearance of Bd when recaptured in the warm season, and many remained Bd-negative or maintained very low loads, suggesting rapid infection clearance. These findings indicate that the analyzed population can persist despite the presence of the aquatic pathogen. Identifying the microclimatic factors that enable hosts to eliminate Bd infections, or alternatively, promote pathogen persistence in the environment, is crucial for understanding population resilience and informing wildlife disease management strategies.

papers.title: Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus detection system established based on the multienzyme isothermal rapid amplification (MIRA) method.
papers.abstract: Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus (IHNV) is an important pathogen of salmonid fish. In this study, a multienzyme isothermal rapid amplification (MIRA) assay targeting a conserved region of the IHNV N gene was established for rapid detection. The performance of the assay was evaluated using IHNV RNA standards, and further compared with digital PCR (dPCR) using 8 IHNV isolates, 12 cell culture supernatants, and 67 tissue samples from rainbow trout suspected of IHNV infection. The MIRA assay produced detectable signals within approximately 20 min. A detection rate of 100% was achieved at 102 copies μl-1 using RNA standards. The assay successfully detected all 8 IHNV isolates and showed no cross-reaction with non-target fish viruses. For cell culture supernatants and tissue samples, the MIRA assay showed a high level of agreement with dPCR results. These findings indicate that the MIRA assay may serve as a rapid and practical method for IHNV detection, particularly for on-site screening and preliminary diagnosis in resource-limited settings.

papers.title: Air pollution is associated with a distinct pathogen spectrum in community-acquired pneumonia: a prospective multicentre cohort study.
papers.abstract: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is the leading cause of death due to infection worldwide, with its incidence and disease course influenced by air pollution exposure. Little is known about how air pollution influences microbiological findings in patients with CAP. Patients were recruited from a prospective, multicentre study of CAP (CAPNETZ). Air pollution data were collected at the city level considering data up to one month before inclusion. Associations with sputum pathogen detection and cell counts were tested using generalised linear mixed-effects logistic regression models adjusting for clinical confounders, centre-level heterogeneity and meteorological data. Internal validation was performed using an Ensemble Feature Selection (EFS) approach. Among 4,446 eligible patients with available sputum samples, a potential pathogen was detected in 1,581 patients, while complete sputum-cell-count data were available for 4,014 patients. Detection of Streptococcus pneumoniae was associated with previous higher exposure to sulphur dioxide (SO 2 ) (OR 1.75, p = 0.008) and carbon monoxide (CO) (OR 1.57, p = 0.02). Escherichia coli was more frequently detected in patients who were exposed to elevated levels of nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) (OR 2.75, p = 0.004) and higher temperature (OR 1.51, p = 0.03), whereas increased fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) exposure (OR 0.37, p = 0.001) was linked to reduced detection. Furthermore, SO 2 exposure influenced the likelihood of obtaining a diagnostically relevant sputum culture and was associated with higher odds of detecting a high leucocyte count (OR 1.18, p = 0.02). Results were largely corroborated by EFS, particularly for S. pneumoniae and E. coli detection. Exposure to air pollution was associated with a distinct pathogen spectrum in patients with CAP. These findings may have implications for the interpretation of microbiological data in an epidemiological and clinical context and highlight the importance of considering air pollution exposure as a confounding factor. Further validation in cohorts with high-quality environmental, microbiological and antimicrobial resistance data is needed. Registry: German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS), DRKS-ID: DRKS00005274, Registration date: 2013-09-11.

papers.title: Site-specific outcomes and genomics in metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
papers.abstract: Clinical and molecular features of pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) according to involved metastatic sites have not been well characterized. We used the Foundry platform to query information for patients with metastatic PDAC at MD Anderson Cancer Center. Involved metastatic sites were extracted using natural language processing from imaging reports and verified by chart reviews. Overall survival (OS) and next-generation sequencing (NGS) data were analyzed. In a cohort of 1095 patients (median overall survival [OS]: 22.8 months), lung-only metastasis was associated with longer median OS (57.6 months, P < .0001). Patients with metastases not involving the liver had OS of 41.3 months, while liver-only (19.5 months) and multiple sites including liver (19.3 months) had the poorest survival. TP53 mutation rates were higher in liver-involved groups (84-85%) vs lung-only (73%) and non-liver metastases (67%, P < .0001). Lower rates of GNAS mutations were detected in liver-only (5%) and liver-involved (2%) cases, and higher in lung-only (8%) and non-liver (10%, P < .01). The frequency of KRAS mutation and mutant allele distribution were not significantly different in tissue-based NGS. However, in liquid biopsy analysis (n = 240), lung-only metastasis showed the lowest mutation detection (50%), TP53 (23%) and KRAS (10%), compared to liver-only detection rates of 65%, 46%, and 52%, respectively (P values: .009, .02, <.001). Patients with PDAC without liver metastasis have significantly improved OS and lower rates of TP53 mutation. Patients with lung-only metastasis had longer OS, a lower liquid-biopsy positivity rate, and a lower rate of KRAS detection by liquid biopsy; because liquid biopsy may under-detect KRAS in lung-only disease, tumor-tissue sequencing should be prioritized in these patients as KRAS-directed therapies emerge.

papers.title: Single-cell CRISPR screen maps epigenetic regulators of lineage specification and malignancies in human HSPCs.
papers.abstract: Mapping how genetic perturbations influence cell fate is key to understanding human development and disease. Here, we developed a massively parallel single-cell CRISPR (scCRISPR) screening platform in primary human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), profiling 322 regulators across 172,382 single-perturbed cells. The resulting multi-layered regulatory framework captured known associations and enabled functional annotation of regulator-phenotype relationships. Specifically, our atlas revealed that regulators acted within perturbation clusters to govern distinct gene programs that shaped cell fate. As proof of concept, we illustrated several examples. SMYD3 emerged as a negative regulator of long-term regenerative capacity. Analysis of lineage output further identified KMT5B, TRIM24, SETD7, and NSD3 as regulators associated with lineage-biased outputs. Finally, integration with clinical datasets identified PRDM10 as a candidate dependency in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This work establishes a scalable functional genomics platform in a primary human stem cell system.

papers.title: Integrating clinical diagnostics with interventional genetics for neurodevelopmental disorders.
papers.abstract: Interventional genetics (IG) refers to the development of therapies aimed at treating the underlying genetic cause of disease. Diagnostic sequencing has advanced to the point where genetic results can be returned within weeks, meaning that therapeutically actionable variants associated with specific diseases could be developed immediately after diagnosis. Here, we describe 81 probands with a neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and family matched controls with full genotype/phenotype information and biobanked stem cells, most of which are consented for sharing. We outline a rapid and scalable pipeline for induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) generation directly from clinical collection, without the need for peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) storage, paired with induction to neurons. We provide a proof of principle for rapid creation of oligonucleotide therapeutics for Kleefstra syndrome. This work introduces a cohort of individuals with NDDs and an implemental pipeline to integrate IG with clinical diagnostics for NDDs. This information documents our experience and provides useful details for clinical centers interested in integrating IG for NDDs with diagnostic sequencing.

papers.title: Identification of CD40 as the target of artemisinin via targeted degradomics for ulcerative colitis.
papers.abstract: Current drugs for ulcerative colitis often face challenges such as significant side effects, high costs, and tendency to induce drug resistance. Repurposing existing drugs is a promising approach that builds on their known safety and efficacy profiles. Artemisinin (Art), a first-line antimalarial agent, shows anti-inflammatory activity. Malaria infection is frequently accompanied by severe intestinal inflammation and barrier disruption, pathological features that share similarities with ulcerative colitis. However, Art's precise anti-inflammatory mechanism and its therapeutic efficacy in ulcerative colitis remain unclear. In this study, using a DSS-induced ulcerative colitis mouse model, we confirmed that Art significantly ameliorates colitis symptoms and restores intestinal barrier function. Mechanistically, we used PROTAC-based targeted degradomics and identified the immunomodulatory protein CD40 as a candidate target of Art. Art treatment was associated with reduced CD40-TRAF6 interaction, suppression of downstream NF-κB and MAPK inflammatory signaling, and decreased release of inflammatory cytokines. This study provides a novel drug candidate and mechanistic foundation for the application of Art in the treatment of ulcerative colitis.

papers.title: Genetic data sharing by clinical laboratories in Canada: A position statement by the Canadian College of Medical Geneticists.
papers.abstract: Next-generation sequencing has transformed diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment across rare disease, cancer, immunology, and infectious disease. As variant interpretation may evolve with emerging evidence, sharing genetic data is essential to improve diagnostic accuracy and advance genomic medicine. However, practical guidance for implementing clinical genetic data sharing remains limited. The Canadian College of Medical Geneticists (CCMG), therefore, developed national guidance to support secure, ethical, and effective genetic data sharing by Canadian clinical laboratories. An ad hoc CCMG working group with broad geographic and disciplinary representation developed the initial framework of this guidance through six meetings. Members included clinical laboratory geneticists, genomics specialists, a legal expert, a clinical geneticist, and a genetic counselor. The process drew on expert consensus (including patient and family perspectives), existing frameworks, and relevant peer-reviewed evidence, followed by iterative external review. Reporting was informed by the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation II (AGREE II) framework. The guidance provides recommendations to support genetic data sharing by Canadian clinical laboratories. It addresses benefits, risks, and ethical considerations, with emphasis on proportionality, privacy, and governance. Recommendations include approaches to sharing diverse genetic data types, establishing institutional policies, and addressing implementation barriers. This guidance aims to align Canadian clinical laboratory data-sharing practices with international standards and improve diagnostic accuracy, equity, and innovation in genomic medicine. By emphasizing ethical principles, proportionality, and governance, it seeks to enable responsible data sharing; strengthen trust among patients, families, and professionals; and contribute to the broader global genomic data ecosystem.

papers.title: Comparison of Next-Generation Sequencing and Quantitative PCR Methodologies for Quantification of Fungicide Resistance in Mixed Samples of Colletotrichum siamense .
papers.abstract: Measuring the frequency of fungicide resistance alleles in pathogen populations is critical for understanding resistance spread and severity. TaqMan quantitative PCR (qPCR) is a standard method for allele quantification, whereas next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies offer an alternative for high-resolution detection. Because studies exploring NGS for this purpose are limited, the objective of this study was to compare the accuracy and feasibility of Illumina NGS amplicon sequencing with that of a previously validated TaqMan qPCR assay to quantify resistance alleles to thiophanate-methyl fungicide in a set of mixed Colletotrichum siamense DNA samples. For validation, a set with known frequencies of resistance to thiophanate-methyl was used as a control. Both the NGS- and qPCR-based methods were highly precise, with an R 2 of 0.99 and 0.97, respectively, for the C. siamense DNA samples with known resistance frequencies. However, with the samples of unknown resistance frequencies that were collected from detached blueberry fruit assays, the NGS method demonstrated more variability than the TaqMan method ( P < 0.001). This variability was likely associated with low target DNA concentration and the presence of host and nontarget fungal DNA, which reduced PCR efficiency. This study highlighted strengths and weaknesses of both technologies and important assay design considerations. It was concluded that NGS-based methodologies may be preferential for large sample sizes and for detecting multiple or novel mutations within a region, whereas the qPCR assay can be more efficient for rapid quantification of known alleles.

papers.title: A global survey of type I secretion systems and the substrates in Gram-negative bacteria.
papers.abstract: Type I secretion system (T1SS) is a special device employed by Gram-negative bacteria, which only contains three components but can mediate the transport of proteins through two cell membranes. Despite their important functions, the true distribution and diversity of T1SSs in Gram-negative bacteria remain unclear. Here, we started from annotating and clustering 50 sets of T1SSs with experimentally validated functions, followed by comprehensive screening of T1SSs from the genomes of 2996 representative bacterial strains with a homology-based detection strategy combined with gene organization analysis. In total, we found 4967 highly confident sets of T1SSs from 2037 strains, encompassing 13 phyla, 357 genera and 901 species. The T1SSs were divided into nine clusters, while Salmonella contains most of the clusters, among which many are specific to the genus. To more comprehensively and precisely identify T1SS substrate proteins (T1SPs), the evolutionary features of validated T1SPs were observed and used to expand the size of high-confidence T1SPs. We also trained multiple traditional machine-learning models, ensemblers, and protein language models to predict T1SPs. Comparisons by a cross-validation strategy and an independent testing dataset both demonstrated the superior performance of a Mamba-based model (T1SEstacker 3.0) over other machine-learning or language models, ensemblers and other state-of-the-art tools. We further applied the model to screen the T1SPs and observed their distribution across the representative bacterial genomes. In summary, the study made a systematic survey on T1SSs and their substrate proteins, providing important resources for the community studying bacterial T1SSs and other protein secretion systems, secreted proteins and virulence.

papers.title: A 16-year retrospective investigation of granulomatous liver injury in immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients at a tertiary care center.
papers.abstract: Recent data on the underlying causes of granulomatous liver injury in the United States remain limited. In this study, we provide updated tertiary care center data on the causes of hepatic granulomas and evaluate the use of histochemical and molecular diagnostics to identify infectious organisms. We retrospectively reviewed 251 cases of hepatic granulomas (2009-2024) stratified by patient immune status. Additionally, we evaluated 6-year retrospective data from 2 institutions to determine the yield of broad-range molecular testing for infectious diseases. Causes of the 251 cases included idiopathic (31%), autoimmune disease (20%), steatohepatitis (19%), sarcoidosis (10%), infection (8%), and drug reaction (4%). A subset (9%) of idiopathic cases showed features highly suspicious for infection, but standard infectious stains were unrevealing, and none were initially sent for molecular testing. Retrospective evaluation of send-out pathogen molecular testing across both institutions revealed organism detection in 32% (12/37) and 50% (4/8) of highly suspicious cases, respectively. Increasing clinicopathologic suspicion correlated positively with successful molecular pathogen identification and inversely with false-positive contamination rates. Molecular testing is frequently underused by pathologists in the workup of granulomatous hepatitis. Pathologists should proactively leverage molecular diagnostics to optimize clinical decision-making when standard histochemical stains are unrevealing.

papers.title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis.
papers.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world's deadliest pathogen 1 . Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations 2,3 . Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis.
