These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein-protein interaction predictions 4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.

papers.title: Enteric infection and childhood stunting: strengthening causal inference from heterogeneous evidence.
papers.abstract: Laboratory detection of enteropathogens is associated with stunting in observational studies, but the pooled odds ratio does not estimate the effect of infection prevention or treatment on an individual child. Pathogen-domain and age-stratified estimates should not be read as equivalent causal effects; current data cannot reliably distinguish organisms, and environmental enteric dysfunction remains a hypothesized mediator, highlighting the need for prospective, longitudinal research to clarify causality. Prevention should integrate nutrition, infection control, and community-level environmental measures in the first 1000 days; empiric treatment of asymptomatic carriage is not supported, and prospective cohorts plus intervention trials are needed.

papers.title: The Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing Network to accelerate research in rare and understudied cancers.
papers.abstract: The genomic characterization of cancers has considerably advanced research and clinical practice. However, critical gaps remain, including limited knowledge of tumor profiles in rare cancers and populations understudied in genomic research and insufficient integration of genomic, clinical and epidemiologic data. This Perspective highlights the Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing (PE-CGS) Network, established by the US National Cancer Institute to address knowledge gaps in rare and understudied cancers. PE-CGS comprises five research centers supported by a coordinating center and guided by an external advisory panel. Collaborations across PE-CGS are grounded in shared values of participant-centeredness, engagement, access, collaboration and innovation. Activities emphasize participant engagement throughout the research process, including the return of results and collection of clinical and epidemiologic data alongside paired tumor/germline sequencing. PE-CGS demonstrates how engagement, return of results and comprehensive data collection can be integrated to support participant-centered cancer genomics research and accelerate research in rare and understudied cancers.
authors: Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing (PE-CGS) Network

papers.title: Phenotypic and genomic characterization of five novel Klebsiella bacteriophages: Exploring the relationship between spot-lysis patterns and host defense systems.
papers.abstract: Individual Klebsiella phages typically exhibit narrow host ranges; novel phages must therefore continue to be isolated and characterized to assemble phage therapy cocktails. However, the determinants governing host range remain unclear. To characterize five novel Klebsiella phages and examine relationships between their spot-lysis profiles and strain genotypes or host defense repertoires. Five sewage-derived phages were morphologically characterized, and their complete genomes were determined. Spot lysis was assessed against 249 clinical isolates of the Klebsiella pneumoniae species complex (KpSC). Genotypes, virulence and resistance determinants, and anti-phage defense systems were identified from draft genomes using Kleborate and DefenseFinder. Two phages were Myovirus-like and three Siphovirus-like, representing novel species within Jiaodavirus and Sugarlandvirus, and the known species Slopekvirus matisse. Overall, 160 of 249 isolates (64.3%) showed spot lysis with at least one phage; ΦKpT256 produced spot lysis in 137 isolates (55.0%), comparatively broad for a single phage. Spot lysis extended across diverse K/O loci, sequence types, and virulence/resistance profiles. Although 2619 defense systems of 156 types were identified, descriptive comparison revealed no obvious one-to-one correspondence between spot-lysis patterns and individual defense systems. Spot-lysis patterns were not readily explained by the bacterial characteristics examined or by any single defense system, suggesting that additional host and phage factors may contribute. ΦKpT256 and the three Siphovirus-like phages showed differing species-level spot-lysis profiles and warrant evaluation as potential components of a KpSC-targeted phage cocktail.

papers.title: Spatial omics in cancer: a review of computational approaches and vision of AI-driven analysis.
papers.abstract: Predicting patient response to cancer treatments remains a challenge due to tumor heterogeneity and complex tumor microenvironments (TMEs). Modern spatial genomics technologies enable gene expression profiling alongside histological frameworks, but comprehensive analysis and clinical translation of these high-dimensionality datasets will benefit from Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). This review synthesizes computational approaches that address challenges of spatial data by examining deep-learning architectures such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for histological feature extraction and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for modeling cell-cell interactions. We then explore the paradigm of Foundation Models that bridge histopathology with transcriptomics to accelerate the identification of spatially resolved biomarkers, improve patient stratification for immunotherapy and targeted treatments, and advance the clinical translation of mechanistic insights derived from the tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: Cancer-specific T cell receptor discovery using 150,000 clinical genomics samples.
papers.abstract: T cell receptors (TCRs) can enable detection and elimination of cancer cells via recognition of cancer-specific peptides presented on human leukocyte antigen (HLA). We speculated that shared cancer antigens could be recognized by recurrent ("public") TCRs, which might be identifiable using statistical methods. Here, we identified public TCRs against therapeutically relevant targets via computational analysis of large-scale bulk RNA sequencing data obtained from routine clinical genomics testing. Using data from ∼150,000 patient tumor samples, we identified TCR chains that were associated with well-known cancer antigens, including human papillomavirus, mutated KRAS, and CT83. We devised methods for pairing enriched TCR-α and TCR-β chain sequences and validated 44 TCRs across nine peptide-HLA targets for antigen recognition, including potent cytotoxic TCRs. Our results suggest that public anticancer TCRs are common and may represent a new source for the development of cancer therapeutics.

papers.title: Integrated Single-Step Duplex CRISPR-Based System for Point-of-Care Detection of Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Treponema pallidum Directly from Whole Blood.
papers.abstract: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and syphilis are two major sexually transmitted diseases that pose serious threats to public health, underscoring the urgent need for fast and sensitive diagnosis for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and Treponema pallidum (TP). Here, we developed a single-step duplex CRISPR assay that integrated reverse transcription, recombinase polymerase amplification, in vitro transcription, and CRISPR/Cas12a and Cas13a detection for simultaneous HIV and TP nucleic acid testing. We further engineered a fully integrated, low-cost microfluidic chip that consolidated whole-blood sample processing, nucleic acid release, and single-step duplex CRISPR detection. The chip featured a rapid plasma separator with a press-actuated design that removed inhibitors and extracted plasma within minutes without external equipment. The entire process was coupled with a homemade smartphone-based portable device that provided thermal incubation, dual-channel fluorescence excitation, and automated image analysis via a dedicated mobile application. This integrated system enables "sample-to-answer" detection within 30 min directly from whole blood, achieving a limit of detection of 2.5 copies/μL of both HIV and TP and demonstrating 100% sensitivity and specificity concordant with the real-time PCR in 51 cases of clinical samples. This work demonstrates a transformative point-of-care diagnostic platform that combines minimal user steps, equipment independence, and robust multiplex detection for decentralized pathogen testing.

papers.title: Gamma irradiation concerning genetics of Ralstonia solanacearum and export quality in potatoes.
papers.abstract: Potato brown rot, caused by Ralstonia solanacearum , is an important quarantine disease that can seriously affect tuber quality and limit the movement and marketability of potatoes. Gamma irradiation may help control the pathogen after harvest, but the dose used can also affect the nutritional value and quality of potato tubers. We aimed to study the genetic diversity of the potato brown rot pathogen, Ralstonia solanacearum, using molecular markers. We also evaluated how irradiation affects the physicochemical properties of treated and untreated potato tubers. Commercial potato varieties were collected from major potato-growing areas of Bangladesh for pathogen isolation and irradiation studies. Forty-two bacterial isolates were characterized on TTC medium and examined using PS-1/PS-2 PCR, 16S rRNA sequencing, phylotype-specific PCR, and mutS amplification. After irradiation, the tubers were assessed for weight loss, ascorbic acid, anthocyanin, carotenoid, total soluble solids (TSS), and mineral content. Virulent isolates produced the expected 553-bp PS-1/PS-2 amplicon. Sequence analysis placed a representative isolate close to Asian Ralstonia reference strains, while phylotype-specific PCR generated a 213-bp product corresponding to phylotype IV. The pathogen-specific 553-bp amplicon remained detectable up to 5.5 kGy but was not detected at 6 kGy under the conditions used in this study. A reduction in mutS band intensity was also observed following irradiation. The effects of irradiation on tuber quality varied with cultivar and dose. Ascorbic acid and carotenoid contents generally decreased with increasing irradiation dose, whereas anthocyanin and TSS remained comparatively stable. Mineral concentrations were generally higher in irradiated tubers than in untreated samples. Gamma irradiation reduced the detectability of the pathogen-specific PCR target, although this does not confirm complete pathogen inactivation. Irradiation conditions require optimization to balance pathogen suppression and nutritional quality. Further viability testing and genomic characterization are recommended.

papers.title: A single-cell atlas of pediatric undifferentiated recurrent fever reveals candidate immune regulators.
papers.abstract: Children with periodic fever syndromes not attributable to infections, rheumatic disorders, malignancies, or known monogenic autoinflammatory conditions are classified as "syndrome of undifferentiated recurrent fever" (SURF). To date, treatment remains empirical, often resulting in only a partial response, underscoring the unmet clinical need for new therapeutic strategies. To advance the molecular understanding of SURF, we generated a large-scale single-cell RNA-seq immune atlas of 29 SURF patients with more than 200,000 cells. Comparison of patients with three healthy cohorts revealed large-scale metabolic shifts together with a distinct cytokine signature already observable during afebrile periods. This indicates that afebrile SURF cannot be considered a less inflammatory resting state but rather as a distinct homeostatic state. Furthermore, our analysis suggests an NAMPT-mediated autocrine feedback loop connecting the metabolic dysregulations with the pro-inflammatory phenotype in monocytes. This study offers insights into the SURF immunopathology and generates testable hypotheses to guide future therapies.

papers.title: Understanding the impact of co-occurring diseases on aerial hyperspectral detection: A UAS case study with grapevine leafroll virus and downy mildew.
papers.abstract: Grapevine disease prevention and management challenges sustainable viticulture globally. Comprehensive vineyard monitoring is time- and labor-intensive, especially in regions where multiple pathogens regularly cause co-occurring infections. We used a visible-to-near-infrared (VNIR) imaging spectrometer mounted on an uncrewed aerial system (UAS) to monitor two New York State vineyards affected by grapevine downy mildew (GDM) and Grapevine Leafroll-associated Virus 3 (GLRaV-3). Four UAS datasets were collected during the 2024 growing season, accompanied by ground scouting, physiological measurements, and PCR diagnostics for a subset of vines. Partial least squares regression (PLSR) models detected GLRaV-3 symptoms with symptomatic-class F1 scores of 0.69-0.72 in August, and models differentiating GDM-only from GLRaV-3-only symptoms achieved accuracies of 0.55-0.82 after down-sampling. To test whether co-occurring GDM impacted accurate GLRaV-3 detection, we compared PLSR recall for GLRaV-3-only vines with recall for vines showing both GLRaV-3 and GDM symptoms. Across three datasets, recall differences (co-occurring minus GLRaV-3-only) were +0.4, +9.0, and -4.6 percentage points and all 95% confidence intervals included zero, suggesting that co-occurring GDM did not consistently reduce GLRaV-3 symptom classification accuracy. This study provides a direct, field-based evaluation of aerial imaging spectroscopy to detect co-occurring grapevine diseases in commercial vineyards. Our results suggest that UAS VNIR data can be informative amidst the biological complexity of ongoing operational agricultural systems. Early-season disease monitoring remains challenging, and larger representative studies are needed to better quantify co-occurrence effects on disease identification via aerial imaging spectroscopy.

papers.title: Photoelectrochemical biosensor using CoPP to quench PTCA for the detection of mip gene fragment.
papers.abstract: Legionella pneumophila is a harmful Gram-negative aquatic pathogen that causes Legionnaires' disease, and sensitive detection of this bacterium is essential for epidemiological investigation. Herein, a photoelectrochemical (PEC) biosensor based on 3,4,9,10-perylenetetracarboxylic acid (PTCA) as the photoactive material and tetraphenylporphyrin cobalt (CoPP) as the signal quencher was constructed for the detection of the macrophage infectivity potentiator (mip) gene fragment from Legionella pneumophila. PTCA with favorable optoelectronic properties and film-forming capacity provided a strong initial photocurrent response. Gold nanoparticles (Au NPs) were electrodeposited on the electrode surface to immobilize DNA S1 through Au-S interactions. After target-induced DNA hybridization, CoPP was intercalated into the formed DNA duplex, which efficiently quenched the PEC signal of PTCA. Benefiting from the signal quenching effect of CoPP towards PTCA, the proposed biosensor achieved quantitative detection of the mip gene fragment in the range from 100 fmol/L to 1 µmol/L with a detection limit of 33.3 fmol/L. This work provides an analytical tool and shows promise for practical screening of the mip gene fragment of Legionella pneumophila in respiratory specimens with high bacterial loads.

papers.title: Unsupervised clustering identifies candidate metabolic profiles, including an acidotic profile detectable before calving, in periparturient dairy cows.
papers.abstract: The metabolic status of periparturient dairy cows is highly heterogeneous, making it difficult for traditional assessment methods based on a single biomarker to comprehensively reflect systemic metabolic dysregulation. This study aimed to apply unsupervised clustering to identify distinct metabolic phenotypes using integrated blood physiological indicators and to evaluate the prepartum identifiability of metabolically compromised profiles. Venous blood samples were collected from 316 healthy Holstein cows (from - 7 to + 7 days relative to calving) across seven commercial farms in China for blood gas and electrolyte analysis. After data cleaning and variable selection, six key indicators-pH, PCO₂, HCO₃⁻, glucose, potassium, and sodium-were standardized and subjected to K-means clustering. The optimal number of clusters was determined to be three, yielding the following phenotypes: (1) a "metabolically compromised" group characterized by acidosis (low pH), hypercapnia (elevated PCO₂), hypoglycemia, and electrolyte imbalance; (2) a "normoacidemic-hyperkalemic" group with normal acid-base status but persistently elevated potassium; and (3) a "metabolically homeostatic" group exhibiting alkalotic tendencies, higher sodium and glucose levels, and stable electrolyte balance. A substantial proportion of cows already belonged to the metabolically compromised phenotype before calving, and its prevalence peaked during the mid-postpartum period (+ 4 to + 7 d). In unadjusted analyses, cows in this cluster exhibited modestly elevated postpartum β-hydroxybutyrate concentrations (P = 0.001) and significantly reduced milk protein percentage (P < 0.001); however, the BHBA association was not significant after adjusting for farm of origin in a mixed-effects model (P = 0.622), whereas the milk protein association remained robust. These findings indicate that impaired metabolic adaptation in this cluster is more consistently reflected by reduced milk protein than by elevated BHBA. Based on cluster centroids and validated by exploratory ROC analysis, prepartum thresholds for identifying the metabolically compromised profile were proposed: venous pH < 7.25 (AUC = 0.928), PCO₂ > 58.75 mmHg (AUC = 0.956), and glucose < 27.5 mg/dL (AUC = 0.876). Potassium was not retained as a discriminatory threshold because its AUC was only 0.577. These thresholds are exploratory and require validation in independent cohorts. These findings demonstrate that periparturient dairy cows segregate into three distinct metabolic states, and that a metabolically compromised acidotic profile can be identified antepartum. This provides a foundation for early risk stratification; future intervention studies are needed to determine whether targeting this profile improves clinical outcomes.

papers.title: MXene-based biosensors for pathogen detection: materials synthesis, sensing mechanisms, and analytical applications.
papers.abstract: Rapid and accurate pathogen detection is essential for disease diagnosis, food safety, environmental monitoring, and public health surveillance. Conventional detection techniques, including culture-based assays, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), and immunoassays, require lengthy analysis time, complex sample preparation, high costs, and sophisticated instrumentation. These challenges have accelerated the development of MXene-based biosensors as promising alternatives for rapid and sensitive pathogen detection. Owing to their exceptional electrical conductivity, large specific surface area, tunable surface chemistry, and excellent biocompatibility, MXenes have emerged as attractive two-dimensional nanomaterials for biosensing applications. This review summarizes recent advances in MXene-based biosensors for pathogen detection, covering synthesis strategies, physicochemical properties, recognition elements, signal transduction mechanisms, and practical applications. Both top-down and bottom-up synthesis approaches are discussed to highlight their influence on MXene properties. The roles of antibodies, aptamers, nucleic acids, peptides, and molecularly imprinted polymers are critically examined, together with electrochemical, optical, fluorescence, and electrochemiluminescence sensing strategies. Furthermore, applications in food safety, environmental monitoring, clinical diagnostics, and wearable sensing devices are reviewed. Despite remarkable progress, challenges related to oxidation stability, restacking, poor long-term storage, batch-to-batch reproducibility, and scalable synthesis remain. These represent significant disadvantages of MXenes compared with conventional nanomaterials. Finally, future perspectives focus on green synthesis, multifunctional nanocomposites, wearable biosensors, and artificial intelligence-assisted data analysis. This review provides a comprehensive perspective on MXene-based biosensors and their potential for next-generation pathogen detection technologies.

papers.title: Cyperus scariosus- mediated synthesis of nickel-based nanomaterials for photocatalytic methylene blue degradation, antibacterial and antioxidant activities.
papers.abstract: The root extract of Cyperus scariosus (C. scariosus) was prepared in water and it was used for the synthesis of a nanomaterial based on nickel. The synthesized nanomaterial was tested for its photocatalytic, antibacterial and antioxidant properties. The maximum absorption wavelength obtained by the UV-visible analysis was ∼292 nm, with an apparent optical transition of ∼3.6 eV. The presence of crystalline features containing nickel and oxygen was confirmed by XRD, FTIR and EDX; however, unambiguous assignment of the reflection at 2θ = 32.58° was not possible and no phase purity was claimed. The image resolved features by SEM ranged from ca. 5-60 nm with a fitted distribution center of 33.5 ± 0.4 nm while the average hydrodynamic diameter by DLS was ca. 45 nm. The electrostatic colloidal stabilization was found to be limited with a zeta potential of around -14 mV. The material under sunlight irradiation resulted in about 96% of absorption reduction of methylene-blue in 50 min. The pseudo-first order rate constant was found to be 0.0153 min-1 at 298 K and 0.0286 min-1 at 343 K with an apparent activation energy of 12.04 kJ mol-1. After 5 reuses around 80% of degradation activity was maintained. An anti-bacterial and anti-oxidant response was also seen, and scavenger experiments indicated that more than one reactive species was involved, but did not identify a specific pathway. The results indicate that plant-based nickel-based materials could be used to treat dye-contaminated water, and suggest that more research is needed in this area. In the future, the mineralization, nickel release, ecotoxicity and performance of the system should be assessed in actual wastewater.

papers.title: Culture-negative peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis rates are decreased with water lysis but not 16S rRNA gene sequencing.
papers.abstract: ObjectivesA successful peritoneal dialysis (PD) programme should aim to have low peritoneal dialysis-associated peritonitis (PDAP) rates. Identification of the microbial organism enables targeted antibiotic treatment and allows for a root cause analysis to be performed. Culture-negative (CN) peritonitis presents a more challenging scenario whereby empirical treatment for Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms is commenced for 14 days, with Gram-negative cover discontinued based upon clinical response. In accordance with ISPD recommendations, we conducted a clinical quality improvement project in 2018 to decrease our culture-negative PDAP.MethodsFrom 2018 to 2021, our department had 336 cases of PDAP. The introduction of a water-lysis step and the application of 16S rRNA gene sequencing were implemented to reduce culture-negative PDAP.ResultsThere were 336 cases of PDAP between 2018 and 2021. In total, 135 cases occurred prior to the initiation of the water lysis step and 201 cases occurred after the introduction of the water lysis step and 16S rRNA sequencing. The rate of culture-negative PDAP prior to our change in PD effluent culture methodology was 33% (45/135); following changes to include a water lysis step and an increase in sample volume, the rate of culture-negative PDAP significantly fell to 20% (41/201) ( p < 0.01). 16S rRNA, using Sanger sequencing of culture-negative samples, did not significantly increase pathogen detection. Five out of 6 samples remained CN in the pre-water lysis step group, and 17 out of 23 samples also remained CN in the post-water lysis group ( p = 0.61).ConclusionsIntroduction of water lysis of peritoneal effluent significantly decreased culture-negative peritonitis rates, thus increasing organism identification and allowing for targeted antimicrobial therapy.

papers.title: Comparative and Sex-Specific Assessment of Proteomics, Clinical, and Genomic Data on Visceral Adipose Tissue Volume Using Machine Learning in UK Biobank: Advancing Precision Medicine.
papers.abstract: Visceral adiposity is a key driver of insulin resistance, which in turn is a strong risk factor for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases. We investigated the overall and sex-specific associations between plasma proteomics and visceral adipose tissue volume, and their intersection with clinical and genomic data to identify critical candidate proteins for visceral adiposity possibly linked to insulin resistance. We analyzed data from UK Biobank participants, using multistep machine learning to establish linear and nonlinear associations. The combined model, integrating clinical, proteomic, and polygenic data, accounted for 67% of visceral adipose tissue variance. Our research revealed significant protein interactions with environmental factors and identified sex-specific proteins correlated with visceral adipose tissue variance in both males and females. The findings suggest that a small number of plasma proteins explain a significant portion of the variance of visceral adipose tissue beyond nonproteomic measures, offering a potential single-source, personalized measurement of visceral adiposity that is easily accessible and may facilitate improved prediction and understanding of the biology of insulin resistance.

papers.title: Pathogen-specific positron emission tomography for Enterobacterales bone infection.
papers.abstract: Gram-negative bone infections involving Enterobacterales group of bacteria pose a growing concern, especially for orthopaedic surgeries and diabetic ulcers. Current imaging methods either identify morphological changes by CT and MRI, or inflammation, using white blood cell scans or 2-deoxy-2-[ 18 F]fluoro-d-glucose ([ 18 F]-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET). While valuable, these are not specific, resulting in delayed diagnoses. PET/CT using 2-deoxy-2-[ 18 F]fluoro-d-sorbitol ([ 18 F]-FDS) is a novel method for detecting living Enterobacterales bacteria in vivo, via a conserved sorbitol-specific bacterial pathway. In this study, we aim to evaluate [ 18 F]-FDS PET/CT for detection and monitoring of Enterobacterales bone infection in a mouse model. We adapted a murine model of Gram-positive implant-associated spine infection to a Gram-negative infection model. We compared microbiological techniques to imaging with [ 18 F]-FDG and [ 18 F]-FDS. We determined the standardized uptake value (SUV) ratios for detection of bacterial infection and response to therapy, in 48 mice with surgical implants infected with either Escherichia coli or Staphylococcus aureus and compared them to controls with surgical implants but no infection. Both bacteria induced substantial bone pathology with reduced bone density. [ 18 F]-FDS PET could specifically detect implant-associated spinal infections due to E. coli with a mean SUV ratio of 2.2 (SD 1.3), which was substantially lower in S. aureus (0.7 (SD 0.2); p = 0.002) and uninfected mice (1.0 (SD 0.1)). In contrast, [ 18 F]-FDG could not differentiate between the two bacterial infections or the control (p = 0.497). Finally, [ 18 F]-FDS PET could determine antibiotic efficacy, and monitor infection over time. We demonstrate that [ 18 F]-FDS affords a highly accurate and clinically translatable detection of Enterobacterales bone infection. This novel modality offers a rapid and specific method to diagnose and monitor bone infections, inform medical decisions, reduce the need for surgery, and limit unnecessary antibiotic use. Similar approaches may be implemented to develop tracers for other bacteria.

papers.title: The two-component system CrdRS mediates sub-inhibitory antibiotic-induced biofilm formation in Helicobacter pylori via bidirectional regulation of transporters PlpA and GlnP.
papers.abstract: Biofilm formation by Helicobacter pylori is a major driver of antibiotic tolerance and treatment failure, yet the signaling pathways that trigger biofilm development under sub-inhibitory antibiotic pressure remain poorly understood. Here, we show that sub-MIC levels of metronidazole, amoxicillin, and ciprofloxacin potently induce dense H. pylori biofilms. Through transcriptomic and genetic analyses, we identify the two-component system CrdRS as a central signaling hub that orchestrates this response via the bidirectional regulation of two ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters. Phosphorylated CrdR binds to AC-rich promoter motifs to directly activate plpA , which encodes a substrate-binding protein that drives exopolysaccharide secretion and matrix assembly. Concomitantly, CrdR represses glnP , which encodes an inner-membrane permease, thereby relieving transcriptional inhibition of the L-asparaginase gene ansB . This derepression triggers aberrant reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, which promotes oxidative stress-dependent biofilm maturation. Through phenotypic analysis of c rdRS deletion mutants, phosphorylation-defective point mutants (CrdR D53A and CrdS H173A ), and exogenous hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) induction, we demonstrate that CrdRS is required for mediating antibiotic-induced stress responses in a manner genetically separable from ROS sensing. Collectively, our findings establish a dual-mechanism model in which CrdRS orchestrates antibiotic-induced biofilm formation by simultaneously controlling matrix production and intracellular ROS generation. Notably, glnP expression was significantly lower in clinical multidrug-resistant isolates than in drug-sensitive ones, whereas plpA showed the opposite trend. These findings provide a mechanistic foundation for developing CrdRS-targeted strategies to combat biofilm-associated H. pylori infections.

papers.title: Age-dependent genetic effects contribute to immunosenescence in Drosophila melanogaster.
papers.abstract: Immunosenescence, the age-related decline in immune function, varies widely among individuals. Although both genetic and environmental factors contribute to variation in immunosenescence, the extent to which age-specific genetic effects shape age-related immune decline remains poorly understood. Here, we tested whether age-related variation in bacterial clearance is shaped by age-dependent genetic effects by measuring clearance of Escherichia coli infection in 175 genotypes at 1 wk of age and 183 genotypes at 5 wk of age. Clearance ability declined with age, but the magnitude of decline differed markedly among genotypes. Age-specific genetic effects explained substantially more phenotypic variation than age-independent genetic differences, and the genetic correlation in clearance ability across ages was modest, indicating that genetic effects on immune performance were only partially shared across ages. Consistent with these findings, genome-wide analyses identified largely distinct sets of candidate genes associated with clearance in young and old flies, including genes exhibiting genotype-by-age effects. Network and gene ontology analyses revealed enrichment for plasma membrane-associated genes and pathways involved in cell adhesion and cell migration. Functional follow-up of 14 candidate genes using hemocyte-specific RNA interference produced limited effects overall but confirmed that nebulosa contributes to bacterial clearance. Together, our results demonstrate that immunosenescence is shaped by age-dependent genetic effects and identify conserved pathways and candidate genes for future mechanistic studies of age-related immune decline.

papers.title: Quantitative Resistance to Aphanomyces Root Rot in Legumes.
papers.abstract: Aphanomyces root rot, caused by the soilborne oomycete Aphanomyces euteiches Drechs., is an important threat to legume crop production. In susceptible grain legumes, such as pea ( Pisum sativum ) and lentil ( Lens culinaris ), the disease can cause total yield loss under favorable infection conditions. No effective and durable method of disease control is currently available. Therefore, farmers are advised to prevent the spread of the pathogen through crop rotations with nonhost or resistant crops, and by monitoring soil inoculum levels using detection tests. Genetic resistance is an essential method for managing crop diseases. Indeed, significant progress has been achieved over the past three decades in identifying quantitative trait loci (QTL) for resistance to A. euteiches mainly in pea, but also in lentil, faba bean ( Vicia faba ), and the model species Medicago truncatula . These advances in genetics research have led to the recent registration in France of the first partially resistant pea varieties. This feature article provides a review of the research knowledge on the A. euteiches × legumes pathosystem, as well as plant sources of resistance, genetic determinants, and molecular mechanisms of quantitative resistance to A. euteiches currently being deciphered in pulse grains and the model legume species studied. It also highlights future research directions for the development of effective and durable resistance in legume varieties.

papers.title: Auditing Biomedical Literature with Blinded AI Peer Review: Where Peer Review Works, Where It Fails, and How to Strengthen It
papers.abstract: Biomedical publishing has grown more than elevenfold since 1991, outstripping human peer review. Unblinded language models cannot audit this literature objectively because they recognize famous authors and journals from training memory. We built BARS (Blinded AI Review System), an automated referee that strips titles, author names, institutions, journal headers, and dates before grading full-text manuscripts on a 10-point scale covering methods, evidence, biology, and reproducibility. We used BARS to generate 1,874 blind reviews across 1,714 unique papers. BARS passed 100% of verified sound controls, caught 77% to 91% of internally flawed papers, eliminated a +0.35-point prestige boost, and more than doubled human referee consistency. Across 320 recent open-access articles (2020-2025) from eight fields, 54% failed on core scientific rigor (<5.0/10; 41% excluding megajournals). Revision at selective journals improved preprints more than twice as much as revision at commercial megajournals (+0.62 vs. +0.30 points; baseline-adjusted p = 0.033), and BARS recalled 98% of unresolved human referee critiques across 100 open-review papers. Across 915 date-blinded papers from 1991 to 2025, average scores fell from 7.6/10 to 5.8/10 as megajournals and template database studies expanded. Blinded self-audits of 238 papers by two senior authors -- and of this manuscript itself -- caught real statistical, control, and table errors in our own work. At four cents per paper, BARS offers a practical quality check for authors, journals, and readers (https://veg.github.io/BARS/).

papers.title: Protein language models learn the underlying accessibility of mutations alongside protein fitness landscapes
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) score the effects of amino acid replacements as pseudo-probabilities, which are widely utilised to map protein fitness landscapes. However, because their training data relies on natural amino acid sequences, these models conflate protein structural constraints with nucleotide mutation biases and codon accessibility. Using the rapid emergence of the divergent influenza A H3N2 K lineage as a stress test, we investigate how base PLMs (ESM-2 and ESM-C) versus fine-tuned versions of these models capture mutational processes. We systematically implement a parameter sweep to explicitly couple (or decouple) empirical nucleotide mutational supply from PLM-assessed amino acid substitution pseudo-probabilities across evolutionary forecasting tasks. We find that base PLMs implicitly learn generic nucleotide-level mutational constraints, an effect strongly amplified by virus-specific fine-tuning. Incorporating explicit mutational accessibility significantly improves the binary prediction of observed amino acid changes. Conversely, when predicting the final circulating frequency of variants that have already emerged, adding mutational supply degrades performance, confirming that selection dominates post-emergence dynamics. Additionally, we perform amino-acid-level epistatic scanning to investigate protein structural constraints in the context of genetic background. This indicates the improbable antigenic substitution I160K is dependent on co-occurring S144N and N158D mutations in the H3N2 K lineage. Ultimately, current PLM pseudo-probabilities are a composite metric that conflates protein structural fitness with historical biases in mutational supply. Explicitly decoupling these independent evolutionary processes optimises predictive accuracy for real-world pathogen forecasting and isolates pure protein fitness for synthetic design pipelines.

papers.title: Prediction of early Toxoplasma gondii infection during pregnancy combining host biomarkers and machine learning
papers.abstract: Toxoplasma gondii is a major cause of reproductive failure and severe gestational complications in both humans and small ruminants and early diagnosis is essential to prevent adverse outcomes. In sheep, congenital toxoplasmosis can trigger early fetal death (EFD) during the acute phase of the infection (days 7-14 post-infection) when conventional diagnosis methods are ineffective. Therefore, this study aimed to identify early infection biomarkers using a machine learning approach to support EFD diagnosis and providing a translational foundation for early diagnostic strategies in human toxoplasmosis. For that, 27 serum biomarkers (cytokines, acute-phase proteins, oxidative stress and hemostatic parameters) were evaluated during the early stage of infection in 22 pregnant sheep experimentally challenged with T. gondii and 6 uninfected controls. To assess diagnostic specificity, models were tested using sera from animals experimentally infected with other abortifacient agents (Neospora caninum and Chlamydia abortus) and validated with samples from 19 natural abortion outbreaks. A four-biomarkers panel, encompassing CXCL9, CXCL10, IFN-{gamma}, and serum amyloid A, achieved over 74% accuracy in the specific detection of early T. gondii infection and 100% of sensitivity when studying natural infection cases. This approach might support the development of rapid diagnostic strategies, improving early intervention and disease management in livestock production systems. Its translation to human medicine could also aid in addressing current diagnostic gaps and facilitate timely interventions to prevent congenital toxoplasmosis and pregnancy loss in women.

papers.title: GPBench: A benchmark framework for genomic prediction
papers.abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) has emerged as a powerful data mining strategy for disease risk assessment and molecular breeding. GP leverages genome-wide genetic variations and phenotypic information through a computational model to estimate genetic potential or disease risk. However, the field of GP still faces several major challenges: (i) dataset bias and insufficient representativeness; (ii) the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and a systematic benchmarking framework; (iii) heavy reliance on empirical expertise for experimental result interpretation, which hinders large-scale and systematic analysis. These issues make it difficult to conduct systematic cross-species evaluation and comparison of GP methods, and their authentic applications. To address these challenges, we established a standardized and extensible GP benchmark framework-GPBench. We first collected and harmonized public datasets from 16 species, covering animals, plants, and microorganisms, comprising 57 traits, 40,821 samples, and 493,821 single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Then, using the standardized datasets, the framework evaluates 21 GP models and provides a unified assessment across four dimensions: effectiveness, sensitivity, robustness, and scalability. Furthermore, we developed a large language model-based intelligent analysis system to facilitate the interpretation of GP experiments and model recommendations. GPBench provides the community with a fair, unified, and scalable platform (https://www.sdu-idea.cn/GPBench/) and an open-source library for comparing and optimizing GP methods, ultimately accelerating the application of GP in life sciences and biomedical research.

papers.title: The Braarudosphaera bigelowii genome reveals cellular remodeling around a nitrogen-fixing organelle
papers.abstract: Braarudosphaera bigelowii hosts the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial organelle UCYN-A, or the nitroplast, but the absence of a reference genome has limited investigation of the genomic features accompanying this association. Here, we present nuclear and organellar genome resources for the cultured B. bigelowii strain FR-21. The assembly comprises a 472.1-Mb nuclear genome together with representative nitroplast, chloroplast, and mitochondrial genomes of 1.49 Mb, 107 kb, and 44 kb, respectively. The four genomic compartments have strongly differentiated GC compositions, consistent with their distinct evolutionary origins. The large nuclear genome does not appear to reflect a corresponding expansion of protein-coding capacity. Repeat annotation indicates that approximately 77% of the nuclear assembly is repetitive, leaving approximately 108 Mb of nonrepetitive sequence containing roughly 16,000 predicted protein-coding genes. Phylogenomic analysis places B. bigelowii within the expected diversity of haptophytes, indicating that its unusual diazotrophic lifestyle is not associated with an anomalous phylogenetic position. Comparative analysis of nitrogen metabolism genes reveals extensive remodeling of host nitrogen acquisition and assimilation. B. bigelowii lacks major components required for nitrate and nitrite assimilation and has reduced capacity to use urea, cyanate, and several internally recycled nitrogen sources. In contrast, ammonium transport and the glutamine synthetase-glutamate synthase pathway are retained. This combination suggests reduced flexibility in nitrogen use and a host metabolism increasingly centered on ammonium supplied by the nitroplast. B. bigelowii also encodes an expanded set of flavodoxin and cryptochrome genes. Eleven of 14 flavodoxin candidates and 21 of 39 cryptochrome candidates contained motifs linked to nitroplast targeting. Together with previous evidence that some of these proteins are abundantly imported into the nitroplast, these expansions point to host-encoded roles in nitroplast redox metabolism and diel regulation. These genome resources establish a foundation for investigating nitroplast protein import, host-organelle metabolic integration, and the genomic consequences of acquiring an intracellular nitrogen-fixing compartment. They further show that the evolution of the B. bigelowii-UCYN-A relationship involved substantial remodeling of genome architecture and nitrogen metabolism in both partners.

papers.title: Few-shot regulatory sequence design with a genomic language model
papers.abstract: A central challenge in generative biology is translating knowledge learned from natural sequences and experiments into designs with desired functions. In-context learning (ICL) is an emergent capability of large language models that allows them to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without additional training, enabling these models to become general-purpose learners. Here, we show that the genome language model, Evo 2, exhibits generative ICL in biological sequence design. Prompting with just tens of examples conditions Evo 2 to generate novel and diverse regulatory DNA sequences without any additional training. Mechanistic analysis suggests that genomic ICL may originate from induction, similar to phenomena observed in natural language. Reinforcement learning leveraging sequence-to-function models as experiment-derived rewards further strengthens ICL. We first validate this approach by generating enhancers that drive cell-type-specific gene expression in three human cell lines. Extending this approach in vivo, enhancers designed using human regulatory element data selectively label layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the mouse cortex with high specificity and stronger activity than existing enhancers. Our study provides evidence of emergent properties in genomic sequence models and introduces a promising approach for improving functional conditioning in generative biology.

papers.title: COSMOS: integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics for mosquito-borne disease
papers.abstract: By 2050, almost half of the global population will be at risk of mosquito-borne disease. Effective response requires monitoring both pathogen transmission and vector abundance, yet these are typically assessed using separate assays with limited taxonomic breadth. Here we present COSMOS (COmprehensive Sequencing for MOSquito-borne disease), a targeted metagenomics workflow designed to reconstruct pathogen genomes and mosquito community composition directly from mixed field-collected samples. Over three annual rounds of a major Australian surveillance program, we evaluated >120,000 mosquitoes in 219 traps, with 98.7% agreement with surveillance data across seven monitored arboviruses, and additional detections of Sindbis virus and the state's first detection of encephalitic Little Sussex virus. Of 137 viral detections, 101 yielded near-complete genomes (>90% coverage) at median 95x depth. Using an accompanying computational workflow, COSMOS quantified mosquito composition, matching entomological estimates of reported vector species (CCC 0.78-0.89). Joint analysis of virus and vector composition identified structured mosquito communities associated with spatial and temporal environmental variation, allowing the ecological context of arbovirus detections to be characterised. Detections during the Murray Valley encephalitis virus outbreak in 2023 were concentrated within a narrowly defined mosquito-community space corresponding to rural communities dominated by the inland S-AUS sub-lineage of Culex annulirostris. Integrated vector-pathogen metagenomics provides ecological and evolutionary context for arbovirus activity within a single scalable workflow for surveillance and outbreak response.

papers.title: Roost: Avian Influenza Host Genomics Resource
papers.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) causes mass mortality in poultry and wildlife, and puts already threatened species at further risk. Understanding differences in host susceptibility requires evidence currently scattered across publications, surveillance reports and genomic resources. We present Roost, a web resource that brings together more than 1,300 publications and reports, surveillance detections, and a catalogue of over 2,000 avian genome assemblies. Large language model-assisted literature analysis and comparative genomics link species, genes and molecular mechanisms to their supporting evidence. Around 51% of species with HPAI detections are not represented in the analysed corpus. Research concentrates on poultry, model organisms, and a small set of immune pathways. Research tracks neither mortality magnitude nor extinction risk; species with the largest recorded die-offs and threatened hosts alike remain largely unstudied. Roost makes this evidence, along with genome analyses, accessible to researchers and conservation practitioners, connecting documented disease with host biology and highlighting priorities for sequencing and functional research. Roost is available at http://josephguhlin.com/Roost

papers.title: Decoding Cell-type Specific Gene Regulation with CellReg3D by Integrating DNA Large Language Models and 3D Genome Structure
papers.abstract: Gene regulation is a core biological mechanism crucial for organismal growth and development. Recent advances in deep learning, coupled with increasing computational resources, have enabled large-scale modelling of gene regulatory processes. While numerous models have been proposed, effectively capturing long-range genomic interactions remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce CellReg3D, a multiscale and multi-modal deep learning framework designed to model cell-type-specific gene regulation by integrating local sequence patterns with long-range genomic interactions. Existing approaches often overlook the contribution of 3D genome architecture and face limitations in combining sequence-based features with chromatin interaction data. Specifically, CellReg3D overcomes these gaps by leveraging a DNA language model to encode sequence-level information and incorporating Hi-C-derived 3D chromatin interactions to capture chromatin spatial organization. We demonstrate that CellReg3D effectively learns epigenetic patterns and chromatin activity states, achieving state-of-the-art performance in predicting epigenetic marks and gene expression profiles across multiple cell types. Using interpretable methods, we illustrate how the model identifies cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms and prioritizes functional non-coding variants. Furthermore, we apply CellReg3D to enhance the interpretation of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and uncover novel potential gene regulatory interactions. Overall, CellReg3D offers a integrative framework for decoding regulatory genomics, unifying sequence and 3D genome structure data to advance variant prioritization, disease mechanism discovery, and personalized functional genomics.

papers.title: Accelerating antibiotic discovery from Earth's isolated habitats through protein language models and microfluidics
papers.abstract: The antibiotic potential of Earth's isolated habitat microbiomes remains largely unexplored. Accessing this resource requires reliable prioritization across divergent peptide sequences and efficient experimental validation. Here we present MicroSPEAR, an end-to-end framework for antimicrobial peptide (AMP) discovery integrating SPEAR, a sequence-structure-aware ensemble predictor, with MicroGrad, a microfluidic testing platform. SPEAR generalized to low-homology peptides and prioritized potent candidates despite training on binary activity labels. MicroGrad simplified liquid handling and shortened susceptibility testing from approximately 18 h to 4 h. Applied to a catalogue derived from 4,480 metagenomes spanning 15 isolated habitat types, SPEAR identified 383,027 non-redundant candidate AMPs, 63.1% of which lacked detectable homologues in reference databases. Of 85 synthesized candidates, 79 exhibited antibacterial activity at [≤]64 M;. Mechanistic analyses revealed distinct modes of membrane disruption. Four broad-spectrum candidates with low toxicity significantly reduced bacterial burdens in a mouse thigh infection model. MicroSPEAR connects underexplored microbial diversity with experimentally validated antibiotic leads and provides a foundation for lab-in-the-loop discovery.

papers.title: V-SWITCH: A single-vector OFF-to-ON fluorescent reporter of live RNA virus infections
papers.abstract: Fluorescent reporters of viral infection are powerful tools for studying viral pathogenesis and host-pathogen interactions. Here, we present V-SWITCH, a highly modular, single-vector, cell-based OFF-to-ON fluorescent reporter that enables robust detection of viral infection in living cells. V-SWITCH is based on a split mNeonGreen (mNG) system employing a release-and-capture mechanism. In the "OFF" state, the mNG3A(1-10) fragment is anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum via a Sec61 transmembrane domain, while the mNG(11) fragment, fused to BFP, is constitutively expressed in the nucleus. Upon infection, the viral protease cleaves a protease cleavage site (PCS) adjacent to the mNG3A(1-10) fragment, liberating it for translocation into the nucleus. There, it complements mNG(11) to reconstitute fluorescence. The constitutive BFP serves as both an expression control and a nuclear segmentation marker for image analysis. Each module in this dual-cassette design is flanked by unique restriction sites allowing rapid swapping of virus-specific PCS, split fluorophores, membrane anchors, and promoters. We demonstrate the versatility of the V-SWITCH reporter for several viruses (Dengue virus, Zika virus, West Nile virus and Human Coronavirus OC43) in several cell lines (A549, BJ-5 fibroblasts, HEK293T and HeLa). Reporter activation enables clear discrimination of infected and uninfected cells by flow cytometry and reveals time-dependent and heterogeneous infection dynamics by live-cell imaging at single-cell resolution. Importantly, we demonstrate the potential of V-SWITCH to support both rapid functional screening for host factor dependencies, as well as high-throughput compound screening to enable antiviral discovery and comparative evaluation of therapeutic strategies across multiple viruses and cell types.

papers.title: Spectral Adaptive Repositioning for Flow-Based Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling
papers.abstract: Predicting transcriptome-wide cellular responses to genetic and biomolecular perturbations is central to functional genomics and therapeutic target discovery. Existing methods assign gene positional encodings derived from arbitrary orderings or static co-expression masks built from unperturbed cells, and cannot capture the functional rewiring induced by perturbations. We present SPEAR, a generative framework built on two complementary positional mechanisms. Spectral positional encoding grounds each gene's position in the geometry of the co-expression network via continuous coordinates derived from the graph Laplacian. Adaptive repositioning then derives each gene's position from its perturbation-conditioned hidden state at every layer, allowing the attention genes exert on one another to reorganize without explicit supervision. Evaluated on genetic, pharmacological, and cytokine perturbation benchmarks, SPEAR demonstrates excellent recovery of differential gene-expression, distributional structure, and perturbation-specific identifiability. SPEAR also captures latent positional relationships that closely map to known transcription factor-target interactions. https://github.com/shouryaverma/SPEAR}{https://github.com/shouryaverma/SPEAR

papers.title: SeverYX: An ensemble framework for robust variant severity classification
papers.abstract: Accurate interpretation of genetic variants in clinical genomics depends on reconciling multiple computational predictors that often disagree or provide incomplete evidence. We present SeverYX, a transparent, rule-based ensemble framework that consolidates conservation, splicing, and functional-impact predictors into a three-tier severity classification ('High', 'Medium', 'Low') through an effect-aware decision architecture. We benchmarked SeverYX against a curated ClinVar dataset of 270,208 MANE-transcript variants (86,161 pathogenic/likely pathogenic, 184,047 benign/likely benign), stratified by molecular consequence, review status, and haploinsufficiency. The baseline configuration achieved 97.6% concordance with ClinVar; at a fixed High cut, 90.0% of pathogenic and 2.0% of benign variants were assigned High. Concordance was highest for loss-of-function variants and lowest for non-coding and unclassified pathogenic variants, reflecting known gaps in current predictive tools. Systematic threshold optimization, combined with the addition of AlphaMissense and REVEL as missense predictors, raised overall concordance to 98.7%, reduced the benign High rate to 0.4% (at a cost of pathogenic High sensitivity falling to 88.3%), and improved the Matthews correlation coefficient from 0.895 to 0.908. These results show that SeverYX offers a transparent, reproducible and extensible approach for consolidating heterogeneous variant-effect evidence into clinically interpretable severity calls, and a scalable path for incorporating future predictive models into genomic interpretation workflows.

papers.title: Massively parallel quantification and prediction of monomeric protein yield in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Obtaining sufficient quantities of purified proteins in their intended molecular states is essential for biological research and protein engineering. Advances in computational protein design have expanded the functional capabilities of de novo proteins and accelerated candidate generation. However, reliable methods for ranking expected monomeric yield of candidate de novo designs, including molecular binders, fluorescent proteins and enzymes, have yet to be established. Standardized measurements of monomeric yield across diverse sequences remain scarce, limiting our understanding of its determinants and the development of accurate predictors for candidate selection. Here we developed a scalable pooled assay combining peptide barcodes, size-exclusion chromatography and mass spectrometry to quantify monomeric yield for over 39,000 natural protein domain variants, de novo proteins and nanobodies under uniform and standardized Escherichia coli production conditions. We used this dataset to (1) quantify the relationship between folding stability and monomeric yield, (2) benchmark inverse-folding methods, (3) evaluate the utility of structure-prediction confidence metrics in selecting high-yield design candidates, and (4) identify sequence and structural patterns in nanobodies associated with monomeric yield and monomer-to-dimer yield ratios. We further developed ESMC-MonoYield, a protein language model fine-tuned to predict monomeric yield from amino acid sequence alone, and prospectively demonstrated enrichment of high-yield candidates among BindCraft-designed binders. Our approach enables standardized, large-scale measurement of monomeric yield across diverse proteins, and establishes monomeric yield as a sequence-encoded property that can be learned, predicted and ultimately designed.

papers.title: Uncovering cross-signal interactions in single-cell and spatial omics
papers.abstract: Individual cells simultaneously encode multiple biological signals in their gene expression profiles, including spatial position, circadian phase, and disease state. These signals can be entangled in complex ways, including circadian patterns that vary along disease progression and cell cycle dynamics that shift along developmental trajectories. While methods to disentangle such signals have been recently developed, characterizing the interaction itself between multicellular signals along with its effects on tissue function, localizing cellular subpopulations which exhibit signal interactions, and identifying potential candidate genes which drive such interactions, all remain major challenges. We present CRISP which characterizes signal interactions in single-cell gene expression data based on the correspondence between the multiple, probabilistic signal-specific projections of the data. Across simulations with tunable couplings and four single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets, CRISP recovers diverse biological signal interactions and localizes them to informative cellular subpopulations and groups of associated genes; CRISP distinguishes healthy from fibrotic liver samples and localizes the loss of zonation-position coupling to individual fibrotic hepatocytes, resolves the asymmetric coupling of TGF-{beta} response, EMT, and cell-cycle phase to specific cell subpopulations, and flags transcriptionally delayed hepatocytes in Plasmodium liver infection. Beyond quantifying and localizing signal interactions, CRISP can refine existing labels, uncover continuous cellular transitions and reveal condition-associated genes.

papers.title: Lung Epithelial TLR7 is a Factor in Viral Replication and Pathogenesis
papers.abstract: Respiratory virus infections are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality of infants and the elderly worldwide. Currently it is not known how Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) vaccination of infants can cause enhancement of RSV disease, highlighting gaps in our understanding about how viruses like RSV interact with the immune system. Here we address this and show that ERK MAP kinase signaling from Toll-like Receptor-7 (TLR7) detection of RSV and influenza, but not human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV3), infections in bronchial epithelial cells (BECs) drives replication of the viruses. Virus infection is detected by pattern recognition receptors like TLR7 that bind to single stranded RNA (ssRNA) viral replication intermediates in late endosomes. Here we report that TLR7 is expressed in BECs and detects RSV ssRNA, causing ERK MAP kinase signaling. RSV and influenza use this detection and signaling in BECs to drive its replication and infection, a mechanism that counters TLR7s role in antiviral defence. Experimental blockade of TLR7 binding or downstream signalling through ERK MAP kinase decreased RSV and influenza replication, but had no effect on HPIV3. RSV viral loads in mouse and human females were higher compared to males, consistent with higher sex-dependent expression of the TLR7 gene from two copies of the X chromosome in females. In a TLR7 gain of function mouse model there was a significant enhancement of RSV replication and RSV eosinophilic and Th2 disease markers like interleukin-5 (IL-5). In summary, TLR7 is expressed in human lung BECs in the lungs where it acts as a factor in RSV and influenza replication and disease pathogenesis. We propose that this is a major factor in determining the sex-disparity of viral disease.

papers.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
papers.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

papers.title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable SI Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generating novel AMPs with desired properties using generative SI (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable SI (XSI) methods to validate the GenSI model and derive biological insights. In this work, we fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. To advance the interpretability and reliability of the generative model, we applied Explainable SI (XSI) techniques. Specifically, we used a probing classifier and a regressor to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we validated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. Overall, these methods provide mechanistic insight into the model's decision-making process, offering a principled basis for trusting the sequences it generates rather than treating the model as a black box. Candidate sequences were filtered based on predicted Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) along with human insights into the structural activities of the AMPs in bacterial membranes, and a final set of peptides was selected for experimental testing. Biological assays for determining MIC confirmed antimicrobial activity in all generated and tested peptides, with fluorescence and circular dichroism measurements providing structural insight. With our XSI approach, we are able to reveal correlations between amino acid sequence patterns and binding properties of these sequences to bacterial membrane mimics, that directly correlate with biological activities in cell-based assays. This builds confidence in that the learned amino acid interdependencies as applied to AMPs carries physico-chemical meaning and is relevant for discoveries of novel AMPs with therapeutic potential. This work demonstrates that interpretable generative language models can serve as effective and transparent tools for rational AMP discovery.

papers.title: Autonomous generalizability auditing of scientific foundation models
papers.abstract: Determining where scientific foundation models generalize beyond their development data is essential for reliable use, but aggregate benchmarks obscure performance limits and rigorous audits are difficult to conduct routinely. Here, we introduce AutoSPECTRA, a coding-agent protocol for systematic generalizability auditing. To inform its design, we reviewed 38 studies across five biological domains and evaluated coding agents, which generated hypotheses and empirical analyses but applied inconsistent standards for judging evidence. We then structured AutoSPECTRA around measurable generalization axes, prespecified analyses, controlled comparisons and independent confirmation. Across four biological foundation models, audits linked performance to protein sequence composition and relatedness to pretraining data (ESMFold2), representation of perturbations in training (STATE), effective spatial resolution (CONCH), and residue-level genomic, evolutionary and structural context (AlphaMissense). Agents also evaluated alternative explanations and rejected unsupported hypotheses. AutoSPECTRA provides a systematic approach to discovering and testing the limits of scientific foundation models.

papers.title: DB-ATRG: The Density and BI-RADS-Aware Triage and Automatic Report Generation System for Mammography
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe growing volume of mammography screenings has created severe radiologist shortages, while standard First-In, First-Out (FIFO) reading queues fail to prioritize urgent or complex cases, delaying critiScal diagnoses. ObjectiveThis study introduces the Density and BI-RADS-Aware Triage and Report Generation (DB-ATRG) framework to fundamentally restructure mammography workflows by automating diagnostic text generation and enabling risk-based case prioritization. MethodsUtilizing the Digital Mammography Dataset for Breast Cancer Diagnosis Research (DMID), we fine-tuned the 4-billion parameter MedGemma 1.5 vision-language model using Quantization and Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA). The extracted biomarkers drive a dual-phase triage algorithm that flags extremely dense breasts (ACR Category D) for supplemental screening and dynamically ranks remaining cases using a calculated Cumulative Urgency Score. The clinical impact of this triage workflow was evaluated against a standard FIFO queue using a simulated cohort of 100 mammography cases. ResultsDB-ATRG achieved significant improvements over the AMRG baseline in clinical text generation and classification, securing a ROUGE-L score of 0.8012, a METEOR score of 0.8358, and an ACR Density Accuracy of 0.6810. In clinical simulations, the optimized prioritization queue captured 100.0% of high-risk malignancies (BI-RADS 4 and 5) within the first 20% of the reading workload, compared to just 19.2% in the random FIFO queue. This framework effectively accelerated the mean rank position of severe cases from 42.0 down to 7.5. ConclusionBy accurately automating report generation and aggressively prioritizing severe cases, the DB-ATRG framework can drastically optimize clinical resource allocation and accelerate the time-to-diagnosis for the most vulnerable patients. HighlightsO_LIA vision-language model (MedGemma 1.5 4B) is fine-tuned with QLoRA for automated mammography report generation, achieving ROUGE-L 0.8012 and METEOR 0.8358. C_LIO_LIA dual-phase Density and BI-RADS-Aware Triage algorithm restructures FIFO reading queues by clinical urgency. C_LIO_LIThe triage system captures 100.0% of high-risk cases (BI-RADS 4/5) within the first 20% of the worklist, versus 19.2% in standard FIFO. C_LIO_LIACR breast density classification accuracy reaches 0.6810, enabling reliable density-based complexity filtering. C_LI

papers.title: Multi-omics reveals selective metabolic remodelling with trace element supplementation in chronic kidney disease
papers.abstract: BackgroundChronic kidney disease (CKD) imposes persistent metabolic stress, yet whether metabolic organization can be preserved under sustained renal stress remains unclear. Essential trace elements support redox defense, mitochondrial function, and intermediary metabolism, and their homeostasis is disturbed in CKD; however, single-element supplementation has yielded heterogeneous results. We examined whether a defined multi-element formulation preserves metabolic resilience in CKD. MethodsIn a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 80 maintenance dialysis patients received standard care alone (n = 40) or plus a trace element cocktail (TEX, 20 mL/day; n = 40). Longitudinal trajectories were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models; endpoint plasma metabolomics and fecal metagenomics were profiled in subsets. A 5/6 nephrectomy mouse model was used to quantify plasma tryptophan-pathway branches and renal spatial metabolism by MALDI imaging mass spectrometry. ResultsTEX was well tolerated, with no treatment-related safety signal, and was associated with modestly more favorable creatinine and eGFR trajectories. Supplementation constrained, rather than erased, CKD-associated metabolic displacement (median |Cohens d|, 0.25 versus 2.09 for disease effects), selectively realigning circulating metabolism toward the healthy state. The host kynurenine branch responded most strongly, whereas microbial indole metabolism and gut community structure changed little. Renal metabolic remodeling was region-specific, with preservation of selected tubular and antioxidant features. ConclusionsTrace element supplementation preserved metabolic resilience in CKD, limiting metabolic displacement without complete restoration. Preservation of metabolic organization may represent a complementary dimension of therapeutic response in CKD. Trial registrationInternational Traditional Medicine Clinical Trial Registry, ITMCTR2026000263 (registered 3 February 2026).

papers.title: A population-based resource for the prioritization of rare variants of unknown significance in clinical genomics
papers.abstract: Rare diseases represent a major public health challenge because they are often associated with severe phenotypes, yet many causal variants remain undiscovered. Founder populations provide a unique opportunity to identify disease-causing variants through the local enrichment of rare alleles. Using whole-genome sequencing data from individuals in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean population, enriched variants were identified and their founder status was assessed through identity-by-descent sharing. Variant impact was evaluated using functional prediction tools without relying on prior clinical classification. A total of 131 founder variants of interest were identified, most of which would likely have been overlooked by conventional approaches based on existing clinical annotations. We developed a web-based platform that facilitates clinician access to the latest interpretation of their genetic variants of interest. These findings demonstrate that potentially pathogenic variants can remain undetected even in extensively studied founder populations. More broadly, they highlight the value of population structure-based approaches for uncovering rare disease variants and improving the characterization of genetic disease risk across human populations.

papers.title: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in newborns with and without neonatal conjunctivitis: cross-sectional study in Papua New Guinea
papers.abstract: ObjectivesNeisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis can be transmitted from an infected woman to her baby during vaginal birth to cause neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum). Little is known about how often these pathogens cause infection in babies without conjunctivitis. The objectives of this study were to investigate the frequency of C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae in newborn babies with and without conjunctivitis and to estimate the prevalence of these infections and the proportion that was asymptomatic. MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study, nested in a randomised controlled trial in Papua New Guinea. At a visit scheduled 1-2-weeks after birth (visit 1), we took conjunctival swabs from babies with clinical signs of conjunctivitis and from a sample of those with no clinical signs. Babies with conjunctivitis received antibiotic treatment. Swabs were tested for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis by PCR after the end of the study. We estimated the weighted percentage (with 95% confidence intervals, CI) of babies with either organism detected and the asymptomatic proportion. ResultsFrom 21st October, 2017 to 2nd February, 2022, 1699 of 2055 newborn babies attended visit 1. Among 310 babies with clinical data and a result from any swab, 97 had signs of conjunctivitis and 213 did not. Where results were available, C. trachomatis was detected in 12/97 (12.4%) of babies with conjunctivitis and 7/211 (3.3%) without. N. gonorrhoeae was detected in 1/97 (1.0%) of babies with conjunctivitis and 6/210 (2.9%) without. The weighted estimate of C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae prevalence was 6.6% (3.8-9.9%), of which an estimated 87.0% (74.8%-93.8%) was asymptomatic. ConclusionsC. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae were detected in the absence of clinical signs of conjunctivitis in about 1 in 15 babies. This finding has implications for estimation of mother-to-child transmission and evaluation of prophylaxis and treatment interventions. Key messagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABS{blacksquare} Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis cause neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum), which can lead to permanent vision loss if untreated; {blacksquare}Little is known about the occurrence and frequency of N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis in newborn babies without conjunctivitis. What this study adds{blacksquare} This study included babies with clinical conjunctivitis and a sample of babies without clinical signs of conjunctivitis and tested swabs using PCR at a visit scheduled 1-2 weeks after birth; {blacksquare}The overall prevalence of C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae was estimated to be 6.6% (95% CI 3.8-9.9%), of which an estimated 87.0% (74.8%-93.8%) occurred in babies without clinical signs of conjunctivitis. How this study might affect research, practice or policy{blacksquare} The clinical relevance of asymptomatic C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae detection remains unclear; all samples from babies with asymptomatic detection tested negative at a visit scheduled 4-6 weeks after birth; {blacksquare}The results are important for research about mother-to-child transmission of C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae and evaluation of prophylaxis and treatment interventions conducted using molecular diagnostics.

papers.title: Who leads Marburg virus research? Gender, geography and funding in authorship, 2008 to early 2023: a bibliometric baseline before the 2023-2025 outbreaks
papers.abstract: Introduction. Between 2023 and 2025, Marburg virus disease reached Equatorial Guinea, Tanzania, Rwanda and Ethiopia for the first time. WHO's 2025 Marburg research priorities make leadership of studies by local scientists a continuing goal. This study describes who led Marburg virus research before these outbreaks. Methods. I analysed 684 English-language Web of Science papers on Marburg virus published from 2008 to February 2023 (5,700 authorships). Gender was inferred from first names with Gender-API, papers about African countries were identified from their text, funders were harmonised by country and type, and themes were mapped to the WHO priorities. I used Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and logistic and negative binomial regression. Results. Women held 35.1% (95% CI 33.9-36.4) of authorships, 41.6% (37.9-45.4) of first-author and 19.6% (16.7-22.9) of last-author positions. Women last authors rose from 15.1% (2008-2012) to 23.2% (2018-2023). Only 14.6% of papers had an author based in Africa. Of 102 papers about an African country, 25.5% (18.0-34.7) had a first author and 23.5% (16.4-32.6) a last author from that country, below benchmarks for infectious-disease research in Africa. Women based in Africa were last author on 2 papers. Of funded papers, 69.0% acknowledged a US funder (24.0% a US defence agency) and 3.2% an African funder.
