WHO priorities on clinical care, outbreak trials, social science and capacity strengthening each appeared in fewer than 8% of papers. An apparent citation penalty for funded papers disappeared after adjustment (rate ratio 1.07, 0.87-1.33). Conclusions. Before the recent outbreaks, Marburg virus research was led mostly by men in senior positions and by researchers outside the affected countries, and was funded mainly by US agencies. This baseline can track whether recent African-led responses change who leads the field.

papers.title: Wastewater pathogen composition in Atlanta, GA prior to and during the 2026 FIFA World Cup
papers.abstract: Mass gatherings can have many impacts on public health, including facilitating the spread of infectious diseases. Alternative surveillance modalities, such as wastewater-based surveillance (WBS), can complement traditional clinical surveillance. We utilized WBS to examine the influence of the 2026 FIFA World Cup (FWC'26) on the range of infectious pathogens in Atlanta, GA surrounding matches held in the city. Samples (n = 102) were collected from three water reclamation facilities between April and July of 2026 (34 collection days) and tested using the BIOFIRE(R) WATCHFIRE Respiratory (19 targets) and Gastrointestinal (22 targets) PCR Pathogen Panels. Primary data analysis included a temporal comparison of wastewater pathogen profiles before (April 1 to June 10; n = 60) and during (June 15 to July 15; n = 30) the FWC'26 across the three facilities using a modified Poisson model with Bonferroni correction. There were no statistically significant differences in target detection between the two periods. Samples collected after the FWC'26 (July 20 to 29; n = 12) were included in a sensitivity analysis which showed a statistically significant increase in SARS-CoV-2 (RR = 3.21, 95% CI = 1.40-7.39; p = 0.01, p-adjusted = 0.048) during and after the tournament compared to before. However, this coincided with regional and national increases in SARS-CoV-2 detection in wastewater, suggesting ongoing community burden. Wide confidence intervals, lack of quantitative data, and limited data collection after the matches limit our conclusions. This study demonstrates the use of qualitative, multiplexed PCR assays for WBS during a mass gathering sporting event.

papers.title: Beyond Haploinsufficiency: Protein Domain and Variant Class Shape Language Outcomes in SYNGAP1-DEE
papers.abstract: Background SYNGAP1-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (SYNGAP1-DEE) is generally considered a haploinsufficiency disorder, yet language development varies considerably between affected individuals. With targeted therapies, including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), approaching clinical evaluation, understanding genotype-specific differences is increasingly important. We investigated whether expressive language and functional communication are associated with SynGAP protein domains and variant class. Methods We analyzed cross-sectional caregiver-reported data linked to genetic reports from the international PATRE SYNGAP1 registry. Of 440 participants, 334 had variants that could be assigned to a protein domain and classified as missense (n=79) or truncating/splicing (n=255). Variants were mapped to seven predefined SynGAP protein regions. The primary outcome was a five-level current expressive language score. Secondary outcomes included acquisition of two-word phrases and CFCS-derived functional communication. Each domain was compared with all other regions within the same variant class using nonparametric tests and age-adjusted ordinal or logistic regression. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results Missense variants in the C2 domain (aa248-392; n=28) were associated with markedly poorer expressive language (median score 1 vs. 2; age-adjusted OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.06-0.46; q=0.0025). Only 7.1% had acquired two-word phrases compared with 52.0% of individuals with missense variants outside C2 (OR 0.07; q=0.0023). Functional communication was also significantly impaired (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.09-0.56; q=0.0052). Conversely, truncating/splicing variants in the PH domain (aa103-247; n=50) were associated with better expressive language (median 3 vs. 2; OR 3.52, 95% CI 1.99-6.24; q<0.001) and more frequent acquisition of two-word phrases (62.0% vs. 31.5%). No corresponding language association was observed for C2 truncating/splicing variants or for variants in the RasGAP domain. Conclusions Language outcomes in SYNGAP1-DEE are associated with both variant class and protein location. The marked impairment associated with C2 missense variants contrasts with the relatively preserved language abilities observed in PH truncating/splicing variants, suggesting that SYNGAP1-related disease cannot be fully explained by a uniform haploinsufficiency model alone. These findings support considering protein domain and variant class in future ASO trials, particularly for patient stratification, endpoint selection, and interpretation of treatment outcomes.

papers.title: Figure format and the accuracy of AI-assisted reconstruction of Kaplan-Meier survival data
papers.abstract: Reconstructing participant-level data from published Kaplan-Meier curves supports meta-analysis and other secondary survival analyses when original trial records are unavailable. Researchers may use original PDF figures or screenshots, which can look alike but retain different information. We assessed how converting vector figures to images affects reconstruction by a language model that can inspect files and execute code. We generated 64 independent two-arm datasets across four scenarios combining 100 or 1,000 participants per arm with proportional or crossing hazards. Each figure was supplied as a native vector PDF and a matched 300-dpi PNG to Opus 5.5 through Claude Code under the same instructions. Outcomes compared reconstructed records with the original observed records: time-averaged absolute curve error through 24 months, error in the between-group restricted mean survival time difference, and error in the Cox log-hazard ratio. Native PDFs had lower curve error in all 64 completed pairs, including replacements for incomplete runs. Mean errors were 0.000029 and 0.1047 percentage points for PDF and PNG, respectively; the paired difference was -0.1047 (95% confidence interval, -0.1194 to -0.0909). PNG errors in the restricted mean survival time difference and log-hazard ratio were small: mean absolute errors were 0.0084 months and 0.0027. Lower resolution and compression increased curve errors; embedding unchanged pixels in a PDF did not restore vector accuracy. Some PNG runs exceeded the instructed revision limit, so results describe the implemented workflow rather than performance under a strictly enforced limit. Preserving vector information improved reconstruction fidelity in this workflow, but the observed differences do not establish clinically consequential changes in treatment estimates. Validation against reported survival summaries and event counts remains necessary. Generalization to published clinical figures and other model workflows requires further evaluation.

papers.title: Multi-agent LLM teams improve differential recall on curated cases but underperform on emergency working-label matching: a two-cohort, two-family evaluation
papers.abstract: Background. Whether multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines help, add nothing, or underperform a single call may depend on the input and scoring contract rather than the architecture; these boundary conditions are unmapped. Methods. We compared a single direct call (Ax1), five personas in one context (P), and five isolated roles integrated by a moderator (MDT) across curated corpora (87 clinicopathological cases, 406 MedCaseReasoning cases, 392 replication vignettes) and two disjoint emergency cohorts from one repository (364 mixed-label encounters; a protocol-frozen 400-encounter disease-label-only replacement, one local serving stack). Scoring was judge-mediated top-k working-label matching. A completed factorial isolated the active ingredient; a symptom-permissive output-contract arm tested contract fit; three physicians rated discordant cases. Findings. On curated corpora MDT improved differential-list recall (top-3: +5.5 points, p = 0.0079; +3.0, p = 0.0079; +3.3, p = 0.0013) but not top-1 accuracy; the factorial attributed the gain to independent generation plus moderated synthesis, not personas. On emergency presentations the sign reversed: in the disease-label-only cohort Ax1 led MDT at every endpoint (top-3 -5.2 points, 95% CI -8.0 to -2.4, p = 0.0008), a second family reproduced it, and bridged cases excluded the serving stack. A symptom-permissive contract shrank the deficit's point estimates by 52-75%, replacement-cohort intervals all spanning zero though remaining negative; the clause harmed no arm. Physician safety ratings were inconclusive (original-cohort gate missed; replacement-cohort rescue contrast unadjudicable, 95% CI -32.7 to +2.6). Interpretation. Multi-agent diagnostic gains are real but conditional: the sign of the effect tracks input genre, and its magnitude tracks output-contract fit. Curated-benchmark gains should not be extrapolated to first-contact emergency text, where role-based teams underperform a single call at seven-fold token cost. The reversal is label-level and judge-mediated; clinical safety is neither established nor excluded.

papers.title: A Knowledge Database of Physical Activity Interventions for Hypertension using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Physical exercise lowers blood pressure, but guidelines provide broad recommendations that rarely account for age, comorbidities, medications and hypertension severity. A structured, queryable resource of exercise interventions for hypertension is lacking, while manual curation is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We present PAHD (Physical Activity for Hypertension Database), built with large language models (LLMs). An LLM screened 2,548 PubMed records through title-and-abstract and full-text assessment, selecting 255 studies. LLMs extracted arms, exercise protocols, participant characteristics, and outcomes, with two LLMs cross-checking study structure and each value linked to a verbatim quote. Programmatic integration generated 17,273 standardized records from 253 studies, one per reported comparison. Against adjudicated benchmarks, screening achieved 86.3% recall and 80.6% precision, and extraction 90.1% recall and 90.5% precision for blood pressure values. A clinician-facing portal retrieves studies matched to patients hypertension stage and comorbidities. PAHD is a reusable, traceable evidence resource for personalized exercise interventions in hypertension.

papers.title: Investigating pathways of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) contamination and transmission in intensive care units: a prospective genomic surveillance study
papers.abstract: Background Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) species are common healthcare-associated pathogens that cause difficult-to-treat infections. Whole genome sequencing of patients has revealed a substantial burden of patient-to-patient VRE transmission in hospitals, with patients in intensive care units (ICUs) at particularly high risk of acquisition. However, few studies adequately characterize the pathways of VRE transmission between patients in acute care settings - a necessary step to identify current gaps in infection prevention practices. By harnessing genomic clustering analyses of whole genome sequences of VRE isolates from patients, environmental surfaces, and healthcare providers (HCP) in ICUs, we aim to reconstruct indirect pathways of pathogen movement to identify patterns of VRE spread and opportunities for transmission prevention. Methods and Findings We collected daily samples (N = 6848) from ICUs in two hospitals over 13 weeks from four main sampling sources: patients, HCP hands, patient rooms, and shared surfaces. Samples were cultured on selective media and sent for whole genome sequencing (WGS). We used genomic thresholds to identify clusters of related VRE isolates and distinguish unrelated isolates. VRE was detected in samples from 20 out of 322 unique occupant-stays (6.22%). VRE isolates were detected from all sampling sources except for shared surfaces. A total of 44 unique VRE isolates were identified, 43 Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) and one Enterococcus faecalis (VREf). Two distinct patterns of VREfm spread were observed: 1) an outbreak setting with observed patient-to-patient transmission and low VRE genomic heterogeneity, and 2) high VRE genomic heterogeneity and pathogen movement between occupant-stays facilitated by persistent HCP and environmental contamination, but no observed transmission events. VRE detection probabilities were not significantly different between occupant-stays in outbreak and non-outbreak settings (OR = 0.63, 95% CI (0.23, 1.83), p = 0.32). However, including VRE isolates from non-patient samples increased the number of occupant-stays with VRE detection from 6 to 20, a 3.3-fold increase, as compared to patient samples alone. Including non-patient samples also increased the number of VRE multi-isolate genomic clusters detected by 7-fold. Our findings are limited because sampling was primarily conducted in ICUs. Due to the combination of short ICU stay durations and imperfect test sensitivity, VRE transmission events may have been underdetected. Conclusions Our findings characterize the complex nature of VRE transmission pathways in ICU settings. Even without an ongoing outbreak, we found substantial evidence of VRE movement between occupant-stays, facilitated by a combination of HCP hands and environmental surfaces. This study highlights the importance of environmental sampling for understanding VRE transmission potential, which is likely to be underestimated using patient sampling alone. We recommend that future studies incorporate follow-up sampling after discharge to better understand the true burden of transmission.

papers.title: Cognitive Performance in Prodromal Neuronal α Synuclein Disease
papers.abstract: Importance: Cognitive abnormalities may emerge during prodromal neuronal a-synuclein disease (NSD), but their domain specificity and longitudinal course are uncertain. Objective: To characterize baseline cognition and longitudinal change in prodromal NSD compared with healthy controls, NSD-negative genetic carriers, and sporadic Parkinson disease (PD). Design: Longitudinal cohort study using Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) data, with first visits from July 2010 through April 2026 and up to 4 years of follow-up. Setting: Multicenter cohort. Participants: Healthy controls (HC; n=244), GBA1 or LRRK2 nonmanifesting carriers without NSD (n=323), prodromal NSD participants recruited through hyposmia or isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder cohorts (n=1640), and sporadic PD (n=824). Exposures: NSD status and clinical cohort. Main Outcomes and Measures: Cognitive summary scores for verbal memory, executive function, processing speed, language, and visuospatial function, and PPMI-defined mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Models adjusted for age, sex, education, and APOE {varepsilon}4 status. Results: Among 3031 participants (mean [SD] age, 66.6 [7.0] years; 1322 female [43.6%]), prodromal NSD participants had lower baseline verbal-memory performance than HC (adjusted difference, -0.20 SD; 95% CI, -0.34 to -0.07; adjusted P = .007); NSD-negative genetic carriers did not differ from HC. No other cognitive domain was lower than HC at baseline or longitudinally. In the primary age-adjusted analysis, verbal-memory trajectory differed from HC over 4 years (P = .009), whereas in a smaller age-matched sensitivity subset through year 3, it did not (P = .62); the baseline difference persisted (adjusted difference, -0.28 SD; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.10; P = .003). Adjusted MCI probability increased from 10.2% to 15.1% in prodromal NSD, compared with 8.4% to 5.0% in HC and 13.4% to 17.7% in PD. The increase was greater than in HC (ratio of annual odds ratios, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.58; adjusted P = .04) but not PD (P = .62). Conclusions and Relevance: Prodromal NSD was associated with modestly lower verbal memory and increasing MCI probability relative to HC, without lower performance in other cognitive domains. The baseline verbal-memory difference was robust, whereas the longitudinal trajectory finding was not reproduced in the smaller age-matched sensitivity subset.

papers.title: Benchmarking Structural Variant Detection in Whole-Exome Sequencing of 67 Multiple Myeloma Cell Lines
papers.abstract: Background. Although the majority of structural variant (SV) workflows have been derived based on whole genome sequencing (WGS) data, they continue to be applied to whole exome sequence (WES) data for which many studies have evaluated their performance in cancer. An equally important consideration that has not been well studied is the impact of cancer context specific features among WGS-derived SV callers applied to WES data. Similar to personalized medicine, not all SV callers are alike and optimal for use with all cancer types and sequence data types. In addition to sequencing related data features, cancer types have embedded features withing the sequencing data that should be considered. Herein, we performed an analysis of SV heterogeneity among WGS-derived SV callers to WES data in multiple myeloma (MM), a cancer known for its genetically heterogeneous nature. Using WES data derived from a panel of 67 Multiple Myeloma (MM) cell lines, we evaluated seven WGS-derived SV detection tools (Delly, SvABA, BreakDancer, Smoove, LUMPY and Manta) for their ability to identify cytogenetically known genetic abnormalities and to characterize overall differences in the number, length, type, and runtime of SVs called among them. Results. Among the seven tools, Smoove and Manta both had the shortest runtime, processing files in less than 2 minutes, in contrast to tools that required more than two hours to run such as SvABA and Pindel. Smoove was the only SV caller to identify a range of SV types, while SvABA was the most restrictive, calling only breakends. All tools differed in the length of SVs called, with SvABA's unfiltered output including the shortest length of less than 10 base pairs (bps), and Delly and BreakDancer's output including the longest, with SVs of less than 1,000 bps. At the chromosome level, SvABA's unfiltered output and Delly's output included 78% and 27.5% of known SVs, respectively, with the remaining tools (including SvABA's filtered output) achieved recall rates of less of less than 10%. By comparison, at the genomics coordinate level, no tool identified more than 20% of known SVs. Conclusions. As all evaluated SV detection tools achieved poor recall rates on this comprehensive catalog of MM cell lines, this study implies SVs detected by WGS-based SV callers on WES data should be confirmed experimentally before being declared legitimate. Heterogeneity in these tools' output lends support to their combined use in practice. Considering that many clinical grade sequencing panels continue to expand their repertoire of rearrangements with therapeutic implications, our results prompt the potential need for cancer type-matched workflows to evaluate the calling of such rearrangements.

papers.title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records
papers.abstract: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

papers.title: EIN-RECAP: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent Summarization and Retrieval of Infectious-Disease Expert Discussions
papers.abstract: Infectious disease experts exchange practical knowledge through clinical discussions, but identifying relevant information across years of conversations is difficult. These discussions often contain differing opinions and emerging observations that are not yet reflected in published evidence. We present EIN-RECAP, an AI-assisted platform developed with Emerging Infections Network (EIN) experts and deployed in beta to summarize and search historical discussions. The system combines retrieval-grounded summarization, citation validation, and hybrid search while distinguishing published evidence from community experience. We evaluated summarization methods across 3,185 threads and conducted blinded expert review on a recent subset. Although a multi-agent workflow achieved stronger automated scores, experts favored a simpler generation pipeline and identified repetition, inaccuracies, and overconfident recommendations in the more complex system. This feedback motivated an ensemble that improved discussion coverage and key clinical points on nine high-disagreement threads, although retrieval relevance remained a limitation. Our findings demonstrate the importance of expert involvement in clinical AI development and show why automated evaluation alone is insufficient to guide system selection.
